was entertaining callers. After they left she remarked to her husband: "I hope they didn't see my walking shoes lying there. They would think me very untidy if they did." "Oh, if they saw them' they probably thought they were mine, answered her husband, in a consoling tone. And she hasn't spoken to him since. Nov SUFFICIENTLY DEFINITE. I believe you are the boy I bought a paper of yesterday, when I 'didn't have change. I owe you a halfpenny. Here it is." Newsboy (who isn't the boy): "Never mind, mister. Keep it for yer honesty! MY DEAREST Noma,

, The following is a smart visting toilet :—Pearl grey peau de soie is the material of the dress, and this is relieved with a collarette and bow in cherry- coloured velvet. The cuirass bodice, laced down the back, is covered partly with a trellis work in steel beads, and partly with a corselet of cross bands piped with satin, and fastened in front with paste or steel buttons. Shorter bands are carried over the shoulders. four on the left and two on the right side, and are secured down on either rounded end with a button. Here is a new organ-pleated shirt, describing an inverted vandyke in front, aka two fint;lnge at the back.

A very pretty tea-gowu can be mude of sea green phodr, end pale blue merveileux silk front and trimmings, or any suitable combination of colours may be selected. It is princess shape, with close- fitting anderfronts joined into the shoulder and first underarm seams. It is fastened with hooks in the centre, and trimmed at the neck with plush. A pleated brace trims the right front to the bust, and one on the left side crosses it, and is fastened with the sash on to the right side. The front is completed from the waist to the foot with a kilt of the silk. The overfronts are cut in one width with the first sidepiece, and trimmer to the side with.. a cascade of lace. The back is trained ten inches beyond ordinary length, and turned under in pleats at the °entre and side seams. A high collar com- pletes the neck. The full elbow sleeves are gathered over a plain foundation, and finished with a frill lined with silk.

Out of doors furs are everywhere, and most jrokets are now trimmed to a considerable extent with some of these comfortable and becoming ins. However' furs are not indispensible on jackets, and the following elegant and stylish ooat is withont it. It is made entirely of sea plus:i lined with satin, but it wo Id look very well in curl or serge cloth, which, h..)wever, would requirP to be trimmed with moludr braid or fur. It is perfectly close•fitthsg, fe.etene4 with hooks in tte centre of the front. Ths hlck is cut with a lap at the centre seam below the waist. Tee basque is cut with ample Iciness to the lower edge. The shoulder frill, to lock well, should be lined with satin or 'silk, and sets full on the shoulders. It is seourod at the neck, which is finished with a high collar rolled over at the upper edge. The sleeves set high on the shoulder, and the upper front edge is gathered u,•-) the seam next the armhole.

Probably you had "no end" of Christmas cards. I had a great many, and was at my wits' end to know what to do with them until I thought of the following ',ler.. Of couriv, I do not mean to suggest that t his is the only, or even the best way of doing up these dainty trt!s, but it is a very good one, and everyone who tett seen my arrange- ment thinks it a great success. It consists in snaking a pretty overmautel with them, but I should remind you that this is only suitable for a small room. Get a long, narrow strip of looking. glass, and let any carpenter frame it in plain deal, quite twelve inches wide. Glue the cards thickly en to tois, letting them overlap each other appal.. ently (this is done by cutting away the °varitype i picots of the underneath card), and when the whole frame is covered with carob, give them a ooat ol transparent varnish. Paint the piece of deal next to the glass, whioh is left bare, ivory-white, put a white mould big round the sides and bottom, and a shelf painted white for ohina and fans along the top. Care of Food.

Every article of food should be covered until it ap- pears on the table. Milk and butter should be kept in air-tight vessels, and kept covered. They both take up every odour flying in the air,and are positively harmful to take into the stomach after standing uncovered for as hour or two, for not only odours, but the animal- culte that fill the air are attraetel to milk and butter. Uncovered jelly i a menacti.to family health. It is in gelatine jelly that expert bacteriologists imprison germs of disease, to watch them prupagate. They seem to thrive better on that kiad of , food than any other, yet 'in two-thirds of our pantries will be found half-used , dishes or glasses of jelly standing uncovered.

Soap as a Microbe Biller. M. Camescasse, a French physician. says that the mouth is the receptacle for a multitude of serms, many of which it is most difficult to sterilise. For this pur- pose," remarks " Science Sittings," " every ' sort of powder and wash has open recommended at one time or other and then abandoned. Better than the most elaborate of preparations is plain soap. ,with which the mouth should be washed every day as thorou2hly a are the hands. A wet toothbrush should be passed over the soap and then be used in the mouth, without any water. The saliva makes an emulsion, and the motith is-filled with sah.ls as soon as the teeth are briskly rubbed. The operation is completed Lay passing the brush over the inside of the cheeks after all the accessi7 Lie portions ot the teeth and gums have been gone over.

Oldest of Babies. The oldest baby in the world is naturally American: It was born 19 years ago in Philadelphia, and is now no Older in the matter of physical development than it was a few months after its birth. The child is the victim of a curious disease or defect which is not unfamiliar in medical science, but this is one of the most interesting cases of the kind ever reported The ! child at first appeared healthy and well developed. It grew and ate well. At the age of eight months growth seems to hays coased absolutely. But it was more than a year old before the parents began to be seriously alarmed. They then noticed that it showed no inclina- tion to talk or walk. Mary Francis remains .practically as she was at eiht months of age. She has not crown, has no teeth, neither talks nor walks. It still lives on baby fool and shows no sign of dawning intelligence. A slight increase in the size of the head and the lips is all that can be noticed. The child appears fairly healthy and cheerful, and has not developed the deformities which have commonly occurred in similar cases. 14,sts of doctors have examined it, and have , been unable to do anything for it. When it was three years old several of them were still of opinion that it I would grow. Now they have changed their minds.

Easily Made Oxford Frames. Oxford frames are often made out ef manufachired mouldings, and the process is very simple. After getting the right size of the picture, we allow .for the breadth of the moulding and the corners (which are generally 1.4 in. or 21n. at each end). The required pieces are cut , off square with a fine saw,and then placed in pairs. Two of them are cut on the face side down to the rebate, to ' allow the breadth of the moulding to be sunk in. The other two pieces are cut down on the back side to the breadth that the moulding is. The pieces are now cut out with a chisel, and, if done properly, this will allow the mouldings to go one into the other,and become level. A large fancy brass nail is fixed in the corner, this covers up the joint, and fastens the two pieces together. The outside corners and ends should be coloured to match, the moulding. There is nothing to keep these frames square until the glass sad back-board are in., It iP, therefore., important that the glass be cat exactly square, and of such a size that it will keep the frame true. Frames of this kind are very easy to make, and look very well for small pictures.

gOllO. "Lord Grosvenor it is, then, who has rescued my prisoners," said Adlowe. "He must have had a carriage. To what place eould he have taken Giralda ?" He pondered the question, but no light was thrown Upon it.. lade Wigby mount his horse and scour the 0.0. i ill every direction; and he him- self, tile Bittlys, sat down by the road- side and. tried to lace the situation. It was clear that his prisoners had escaped him. He had no hope of overtaking them, or wresting them from Lord Grosvenor. He was defeated. He recognised that fact, and accepted the defeat; but with gathering wrath and vengefulness. "I am failing in an my plans," he thought. "It may be that ruin is coming upon me. If so, I will, like Samson of old, pull ruin down also upon the heath of say enemies, He sat by the road-side during the, few hours that intervened before daybreak, his soul the play- ground of a host of demoniac passions. Soon after dawn Wigby came back and reported that he had obtained no trace of the fugitives. The man was startled at the strange silence with which Adlowe received his adverse report, and still more at the great change a few hours had wrought in his lordship's appearance. He looked ten years older than he had looked, a few hours before. His face was haggard and sallow. His cheeks looked sunken. His eyes gleamed from cavernous sockets, and were encircled with purple rings. "Give me the horse," said Adlowe at length, in a hollow voice. "Perhaps, after all, they went on to Pencoed." He mounted and rode over to Poncoed, proceed- ing at once to the railway station. In answer to his inquiries he was told that no such party as he described had madeits appearance at the station. He learned, however, from overhearing a conver- sation between two employes belonging to the station, that Lord Hampton and the Lady Beatrice were at Hamptonwold, and that Lord Trevelyan was spending a day or two with them. A sudden light beamed upon him. "Grosvenor must have taken Giralda and the boy to see their mother secretly," he thought. "They may at this moment be at Hamptonwold I'll go over to the the inn and make inquiries. Grosvenor may have procured horses there." He histened at once to the inn, and questioned the landlord, who replied to him, briskly: "Lord Grosvenor? Oh, yes, sir. His lordship Is taking his breakfast at this moment with his party." "His party!" ejaculated Adlowe, his sallowness seeming to deepen. "Yes, sir—with Miss Arevalo and her young brother. The carriage is ordered to take them to Hamptonwold. Are you a friend of his lordship, sir?" "No!" hissed Adlowe, between his teeth, in a manner so fierce and theatrical as to frighten the landlord nearly out of his senses, and to create in him a belief that Adlowe was mad. "His friend? No!" • . Adlowe strode into the dingy parlour, his soul seeming on fire. "They are going to Hamptonwold, ostensibly as tourists to look at the place, but really to have a secret meeting. with the Lady Beatrice "be mut- tered, hollowly. "I cannot intercept them. I cannot prevent their going. I have played my game and been defeated. What remains?' He strode to and fro, his face looking as the face of a demon. "The game is not played out yet!" he mut- tered, still more hollowly, his sunken eyes emit- ting strange, spark-like gleams. "I have one card left! The hour has come to play that. I have everything—fortune, love, all! I have counted on becoming the next owner of the Trevelya.n estates. Per twenty years I have schemed to that end, and now four lives stand between me and that glittering prize ! I loved the Lady Beatrice. She was in secret a. wife and mother—the wife of an enemy and rival, the mother of his children ! Then I ought to marry her daughter, and thus secure to myself a fortune. There the same fatality pursued me. She grew to love another. She has balked all my plans ; she hal escaped me every time; she sits up with Grosvenor, and !aughs when she thinks howl have been . ,t, Cursed fatalities ! But, as I said, I have one card left to play !" He clenched his hands and shook them fiercely, as if in hatred and denunciation, and his steps lengthened into strides. "I will play that last card now—this morning,' he ejaculated, savagely. " I will prodauu the story of the Lady Beatrice to her father and Lord Trevelyan. I will cover her 'With shame and disgrace. I will break her heart. Ali, who is that?" Ile fancied he heard a f v••i,,e in the hall. lie vprang to the door. opened ji, and confronted

Dereett‘ e The .:e..,eLive V' ag as Fifflw his lordship was bitter grid pariev. Ee I\;tv,.;i the waiter back who was uoio mai to the /Milo:1r, and came in and shui the door. " Good morning, my lord," be said, and his usually 'vacant eyes emitted &dually, a gleam of inte;ligenee. "1 did net dream of finding you here. j have news for you. Geoffrey Trevelyan is found." Lord Adlowe's eyes seemed suddenly to glaze from the midnight darkness of his facial expression. " Found? Where is he ? " The d tective looked startled at Adlowe's strange excitement, as well he might, but be quietly attri- buted it 1,0 a night of dissipation, and replied: " Let.me_ commence my story at the beginning. You discharged me, my lord, from your service on the night when, having discovered the secret re- treat of the Lady Beatrice Hampton, I placed the key to the garden gate of The Evergreens in your bands. There my service to you ended. The next morning with a view to the handsome rewards that had been offered by Lord Trevelyan years ago for the discovery of his nephew, I set to work the case tip on my own account. I went to The Evergreens, and found that the so-called count had fled. " ?" cried Adlowe, impatiently. ; "I' patiently tracked him to one of Lord Grosvenor's country places. He found that I was *on his track, and fled while I was back in Lrndon. He ran across my path at Hampton House, cleverly disguised, and again I missed him. Yesterday it struck me as probable that •he would have left town. Inexperienced people think the country safer than London. I discovered that the Lady , Beatrice Hampton had gone down to Hampton- wold, in the face ot a great ball at the house of - one of her most intimate London friends. I formed a conclusion quickly that the two intended to -see each other at Hamptonwold." , • "And he is in the neighbourhood now 1" "No ; I think not: But he will be here to-day, I am etre. , I was hanging about Hamptonwold , ,yesterday, but her ladyship saw no.visitor except the young Lord Grosvenor, and later, her father • and Lord TrevelYan." • "You are oh the right track, Rush I" exclaimed , Adlowe, with the force of a sudden conviction. ' "Lord Grosvenor is upstairs now with Miss Giralda and Master Fay, and they are to visit . Hamptonwold this morning. Take my word for it, .• there is to be a secret family meeting somewhere in the grounds 1" . . Rush assented eagerly., "And Lord Trevelyan is there !" suggested Adlowe, "full of fury • and hatred against Geof- frey l" Rush's eyes sparkled. "The marquis would pay well for Geoffrey's arrest-=and so ' would If' declared Adlowe with the look of a demon. "Now is the time to make your fortune' Rush and to become the most famous detective in England ! Be on hand at this secret family meeting, with the proper officers and war-. rant, and arrest Geoffrey Trevelyan in the arms of his wife !'" Rush's face began to wear a sunny glow, answer- ing to Adlowe, "I will," he exclaimed. "Not a moment shall be lost. I will go to work at once !" He hurried away, intent on his nefarious task, and Adlowe laughed, softly—a sneering, deadly laugh, that was strangely like a serpent's hiss. "And I," he muttered darkly, "will go on to Hamptonwold in advance, to prepare Lord Tre- velyan for his part. Oh, I will work him up into one of his great rages. I will so inflame him that he will wish to kill Geoffrey with his own hands. Ah, Geoffrey Trevelyan Lady Beatrice I Giralda my revenge is at hand I" He laughed again in that serpent-like hiss, and hurried down stairs, ordering a saddle-horse, his own being exhausted. It was soon got ready; and having further inflamed himself with brandy, he rode toward Hamptonwold, on his evil and demon- like errand.

" Cassell's Saturday Rut nal "is responsible for the statement that almest any board-school teacher in Lon- don can t.II of cases of blackmailing that have been tried on either himself or some friend'. Although these cases are seldom brought into coart, the officials of the National Union of Teachers have, during the year, to deal with several. The opportunity for blackmailing the profession is (owing to one particular circumstance) remarkably easy. All forms of corporal punishment are forbidden to " Assistants." But this latter term does not mean a boy pupil-teacher : it is a technical one, signifying a man who, after serving a four. years' apprenticeshipend undergoing subsequently two severe examinations for his " paresment," is unfortun- stelY, note head mater, though he mac be, perhaps, filty years old,, and have had twentr-five years' ex- perience as a teacher. Hardly one assistant in ten.it is I safe to assert adheres strictly to this arbitrary prohibi- .

tion. Suppose a Man. such as has been iecribed. happens to find an unruly boy whois demoralising his class Reasoning and ordinary "moral punishments "are wasted, for the urchin may have been incited to this cr;:wduct by a blackmailing parent, and at la.t the teact•er is thoughtless enough to raise his hand, perhaps with A cane-stroke of so slight a character as the boy's ; father would ordinarily disdain to use himself. That is the blackmailer's opportunity. He goes to the master (perhaps even to the head), exaggerates, vows his inten- tion.of taking the " assault " into court, and finally 1 demands a sovereign or so as the price of his forbear- ance.. In ninety-nine times in a hundred he gets it; for, guilty or innocent, a magisterial trial, in the oircurn- stances, would mean a master's professional ruin. Schoolmistresses are more frequently the victims ; and cases have been known where one blackmailing mother had been successful five or six times, even going so far as to severely thrash her child for the purpose of obtain- ing marks for magisterial inspection if only she has happened t.) hear of the slightest tap of the cane on the part of the incautious teacher.

div.head: FATAL RESULT OF A HEAVY SENTENCE.
div.p: FATAL RESULT OF A HEAVY SENTENCE.

An ex-stockbroker, named Pachalsky, a Russian Pole, has died in Wormwood Scrubs prison from effusion on the brain. The unfortunate man was sentenced at the Central Criminal Court in December last to fourteen years' penal servitude for forging a bill of exchange for £lOO. At the coroner's inquiry it was stated by the orison officers that Pachalsky had "fretted " very much over his severe sentence, and the doc'or said that his death no doubt " accelerated by mental worry." 'I he sentence which was passed upon him was of ex- raordinary severity. It is such as we usually see im- nosed upon men who are guilty of aggravated man- slaughter or of frauds of the greatest magnitude. In the ease of this unfortunate Pole it was truly a sentence of death.

VIE HERO OF A MODERN "ARABIAN NIGHTS.' An illustrated interview with Sir Richard Tangye appears in the " Young Man" for February. The his- tory of the rise of the famow engineering works of Messrs. Targye Brothers, near Birmingham. is romantic aq a story from the " Arabian Nights." Five Cornish lads working together upcn their father's little farm, .le4loped a remarkable skill for mechanics. They made working models of engines at home in the winter even- ings, while their father locked on dubiously, and lamented the waste of candles. Rut the mother, with keener perception, recogniSed the bent of her sons' minds and encouraged it.. Truly the candles were not wasted. The fourth brother, now Sir Richaid, being physically weaker than the others, WPS educated for a teacher. Disliking the occupation, however; he nhar.- ioned school-teaching at the age of eighteen to seek Hz fortune in Birmingham, taking a situation as clerk in a small engineering establishment at a, salary of fifty pounds a year. After three years and a half, during whih time his salary had been raised to eighty pounds, he determined to start TN DORMERS FOR HERSELF

as a merchant, his aid friend, Mr. Alderman Whit,, or Birmingham. giving him office-room in his plane of business. Meantime, he had persuaded his two elder iwnthers, skilled mechanics to come from Cornwall arid join him. Together they planned and Warted a bucirpEß ta machine-makers, renting a workshop at four shillings ner week. in a hack street behind a baker's f hop. One dark night to their little shall Came an agent of Brunel, the engineer. Be had heard that " Tangves " had in- vented and were manufacturing an hydranlic j‘ck, which he thought might be of use in launching the Great Eastern. Needless to say,he scarcely expected to find what he wanted when ha saw the insignificant workshop. But he Was soon reassured ; the hydranlic jack was prodired, and arrangements were quickly made for setting about the famous launch. This order for hydraulic jacks proved to be the real fnundation of the hnsiness. As Sir Richard tertelv puts it, "We launched the Great Eastern, and the Great Eastern launched us." With improved business prospects the brothers tank larger workshop. at ten shillings a week, and ventured to engage their first workman, with the cantion that they 'could only guarantee him three months' work. Be is, however, still in their serviee. By 1859 the beefiness had increased so greatly that new premises were taken in Clement-st.. Birmingliam,and finally the world-famed Cornwall Works, THE LARORST ENGINEERING astonllS in the world, were erected at Smethwick. A bargeman crossing a held M the Denton Valley,near Gravesend, on Monday, saw his dog run int.) a chalk pit, and then heard it barking violently. Be went into the pit, and beneath a pile of old tin cans he found the dead but yet warm bodies of two boys, aged eight and tgl=n years,the sons of a labourer named Thomas Jackson. Each boy had a wound in the throat. The police were summoned, and in a thicket near the pit Jackson him- self was found. He was suffering from a severe wound in the throat, and died on the way to the Gravesend Infirmary. It is stated ttiat he has been 6 strange "in his manner lately.
A MILLIONAIRE'S MANSION.

The "Daily Chronicle" learns from New York that Mr. Cornelius Vanderbilt, the New York millionaire and railway king, has just opened his new palace with a grind ball. This modest tome, which is to shelter about ten people during six months of the year, and to remain closed during the other six, stands at the corner of Fifty-seventh Street and Fifth Avenue, and has cost its owner £1,000,000. It is of Spanish deafen outside, built of grey stone, with red facings,turrets, and bottle - meats. It is three storeys high,with alofty attic. The ballre:m lathe largest privatei ballroom in New Yorls, being 75ft. long by 501 t. wide, decorated in white and gold Luis XIV. style. The ceiling cost a fortune, and is made in the form of a double cone, covered with painted nymphs and cupids. Round the cornice are delicatelY modelled flowers, each with an electric light in its heart, while an immense crystal chandulier bane from the centre. The walls on the night of the opening' ball were covered from floor to 'ceiling with natural flowers, at a cost of £1,000; and the entertainment is said to have cost the host £5,000. Adjoining the man- sion is the most expensive garden for its size in the world, for, although it is only the size of an ordinary city lot, the sum of £70,000 was paid for it, and a house which had cost £25,000 to build was torn down to make room for the few flower beds.

The late Sir James Lacaita was quoted by Arch- bishop Thomson as the model of self-pmssession, and the instance by which the Archbishop illus- trated this was highly amusing. He and Sir James were seated in the same carriage, leaving King's Cross for the North, when, as the train slowly steamed out of the station, the portmanteau belonging to the latter was observed left behind on the platform. Without a moment's delay its owner put his head out of the window and shouted " Murder" at the top of his voice, at the same time gesticulating violently with his arms. The officials managed to get the train stopped, and came hurry- ing up to the assistance of the supposed victim, only to be met with the blandest of smiles and politest of requests to kindly put that portmanteau in the train. At first they were inclined to be a bit nasty at being thus "done." hut seeing the portly form of the' Archbishop (the supposed murderer) convulsed with merriment, they gave way to peals of that inextinguishable laughter which Homer tells us always greets the coming of Vulcan by the other gods.

There has been a great deal 'of speculation in regard to the recent conference at Hatfield between Lord Salisbury and Mr. Balfour and Mr. Chamberlain. Probably no one actually knows what passed at that meeting except the parties themselves. but I fled that in usually well-informed Unionist quarters it is now taken for granted that the conference had reference to the action of the Opposition upon the Address, and that a definite course has been decided on. In other words.Mr.Chamberlain's views are believed t, Lave prevailed, and it is expected that the Home will no sooner have met than the much-talked-of assault on the Government will be delivered with all the vigour of which the Opposition are capable. For this reason the forthcoming sIITIMIOII4,es tO be issued by the Unionist leaders are awaited with more interest than usually attaches to thpop perfunctory and formal documents, and there will be keen disappointment, among the fighting Con- servatives at all events, if they are nor couched in terms of more than common urczenev.l7lThere is unmistakab'e evidence that the Unionist whips are adopting every means in their power to bring up their fcrces to a man on the opening day. Th.ro is plainly an impression on the Opposition side that the Government will be at their weakest, dur- ing the first few days of the session The Unionists are counting on the absence of some laggard Liberals, and they are consequently limier a temp- tation to strike the blow, if it is to be struck at all, as soon as possible.

• The suggestion that we should continue to eat oysters and run the risk of typhoid fever does not meet with the approval of Dr. Thorne, the principal officer of health at the Lona' Government Board: Tie pointed out in his report on cholera in 1893 that he thought the germs of that epidemic in some cases could be traced to the delicious bivalve, and at. the same time he observed that. the oyster might also carry the bacilli of typhoid fever. Recent researches on the subject have so confirmed hig opinions that he has made strong recommenda- tions to Mr. Shaw-Lefevre that, there should be a special inqniry tonchinrt the cultivation of oysters. Mr. Shaw-Lefevre in turn has communi- cated with the Board of Trade. and Mr. Bryce has consented that such an inquiry should be held, and at once. The Commission, indeed, is already nominated.

The power of the circulating library over the re- putation of an author, end sometimes his temper, reepives a new illustration from a eomolnint. Mr. Robert Barr, the novelist, brings ngainst Mr. Mudie. The point of nis grievance is that two or three years ago he published a stry in an American magazine, in an abbreviated form, to snit the re- quirements of the rongazine ; that he thereafter snent a year in elaborating and extending it; that the enlarged form of the story was cut down from two volumes to one, and its price reduced from 21s. to 6s. to snit Mr. Mndie ; that then Mr. Millie, dis- covering the magazine version.had some old maga- zines bound 'up and is circulating thnt version; and that he sent back to the publishers the 52 volumes he had ordered. The answeris a very simple one. Mr. Mudiets establishment is a private eoncern.and Mr. Barr has no grievance if it refuses to circulate any one of the hooks, tie may have a claim for the 52 conies which were ordered, a question which could be settled in the county court, and there the matter would end. Mr. Barr calls it "rank in- justice" Let him start a circulating library on his Present principles and he will soon find himself ruined by the number of authors who will insist on his buying and circulating their books.

The officials at the Japanese Legation here are anxious to discount the recently-published accounts of the massacres at Port Arthur. They arimit that reprisals took place, but they , deny with Vigorous emphasis that those reprisals assumed the terrible character which has been represented. While in receipt of a series of explanatory despatches from Jcpan, they are awaiting fuller information before they take steps to set the Japanese story of the terrible incident before the British public. That such steps will he taken is beyond doubt. Already a formal denial has been given to the assertionthat an attempt was made to bribe English war corres- pondents; but this accusation, it is comprehended, pales into insignificance before the lurid-story of the black deeds which are said to have occurred at Port Arthur. What may be the natore of the denial which will be given these assertions has net yet been decided on: hut that, a deaial is necessary is the opinion blth of the Government at Tokio and their spokesmen here.

The edition will bt. completed in L.l formightly parts, each for the stirptiz;ngly low stun of 61. lkfictuiLLAN A*111) CO.—" Tie Sphinx of Eagle- Hawk '' Bollrowool is soother of Messr,. Macmilhai's 23. novels. Tile scene of the story i. pitched in a gold-mining camp in South Austratia, but in some respects it differs considerably from the usual run of tales from the Goldfields. To com- mence with, we have the natural roueinea.s of the miner softened by the influence more cultuted scions of a better class and between the two sect,. is woven the incident of the story. Love and villany have their places but the charm which lies in the perusal of the story is too well distributed to single out any phase for special mention. The chief character or" heroine" is a young person who acts in the humble position of barmaid at the chief hotel in Eaglehawk, but she is unquestionably a lady from the first, though the upper ten of the mining community are by no means willing to ad- mit her claims to that distinction. A road-agent and a murder or two contrive to give point to the plot of the story,but as virtue goes not unrewarded so their misdeeds bring their deserts.A large amount of the book's interest lies in its shortness, for without unnecessary "padding" the story is full, and makes the best of all excuses for an afternoon's laziness.
SINGULAR SCENE AT WARRINGTON
POLICE COURT.

MAGISTRATES TO BE REPORTED TO THE HOME SECRETARY. A " MADMAN " IN COURT. The Warrington Borough Police Court, on Saturday, was the scene of some extraordinary and violent be- haviour on the part of a prisoner named James Blair, who was brought up for being drunk and disorderly in Horse-market-at., on Friday night. Blair is one of the worst characters that ever came into Warrington. He has been in gaol nearly all his life for all manner of offences. He has served five years' penal servitude for assaulting an army officer fled the same term for almost killing a warder in gaol, by throwing him over some banisters down a staircase. Terms of 18 months' imprisonment have been quite common with him, and his chief "role "is that of horse thief,which offence he hag been convicted of about 6 tintes,and, new "out/only on ticket-of-leave from a five years' sentence for that offence,having served three years of it in Dartmoor conviet prisms. By the police he is known as" Tom the Devil" and certainly his conduct in court on Saturday morning justified the soubriquet. In appearance he is tall and very powerfully built, and his naturally wild appearance was further enhanced by a thick shock of tow-coloured curly-hair and a face covered with either coal-dust or soot, from the dark coating of which, his prominent cheek-bones, chin and nose showed in relief. When the magistrates' clerk read the charge over to him he emphatically asserted that he was not guilty.—P.C. Woods stated that on the night in question the prisoner was in Horsemarket-st. and anxious to fight with a soldier who was evidently afraid of him. Witness and P.C. Rylatt came up to prisoner and told him to go, whereupon the prisoner threw off his coat and offered to fight the officers. During this recital the prisoner had eyed the constable with something like contempt which culminated in an occasional guffaw of laughter. When formally asked if he had any questions to ask the officer, he commenced directly with his interrogation, putting some very queer questions to witness and growing more and more ex- cited. Not being able to shake witness' statement be suddenly raised himself up and shouted to the bench (waving his arms like a stump orator) " They won't let me alone! as soon as lam out they are at me again. I was 13 months in Dartmoor convict prison and never tad a report I It's all a put up tale! I was'nt drunk at all! I had no money to get drunk with, and never had a drop." The officers, he said,had kicked him in the ribs, and he offered t 4 "strip" and show the marks. Then, suddenly producing a black lead pencil he banged it on the frame of the dock, and bellowed, "I'll write to the Home Secretary this very day! I'll not he kicked by the police." The magistrates, Mr. J. Burgess (chairman) and Mr. S. Chandley, after various and fruitless attempts to stop this now or complaints, at last aucceeded in attracting priaoner's attention, and announeed that he would have to go to goal for 14 dare hard lahour.--Trisoner :" You can send me for as manylastsou likelbut I'll report you both to the Home Secretary! I will, for not carrying out the law."—On being conducted to the steps leading to the cells he halted at the door and reiterated his 1-threat accompanied by a stream of vituperation. The Chairman then ordered him to be brought back, but , prisoner rushed down the steps into the yard from whence it took four officers to bring him alter some •delay, during which those in court could hear loud shouts and threats and other indications of a struggle. On re-appearing, prisoner was without his coat and looked very dishevelled. The Chairman sentenced him to another 14 days, and prisoner said, "I don't care if ynu give me another 28." He was then conducted to the 7 cells, but for some time shouts and screams penetrated to the courtroom from below.

SHOCKING PARENTAL NEGLECT AT SANKEY BRIDGES. X 'MILD'S QUEER SLEEPING PLACES. At the Borough Police Court, on Wednesday morning, bef4ore Mr. John Fairclough and other magistrates, Patrickfiartley was charged with neglecting his boy, Patrick, aged 7, in a manner likely to cause injure to his health..--Inspector McAteer, N.S.P.C.C., stated that the defendant was a labourer,residing at 84,Floward-st., Sankey Bridges. He was a widower, and the father of three children, namely, Jane, 13 ; Thomas, 10 ; and Patrick (the boy present), 7. On Thursday morning last week thii defendant turned the boy Patrick out and told him to go and beg. The boy made his way to Warrington in the evening, and went about begging from door to door. That night he went to the market andaslept under ore of the stalls until morning, when he came out and begged till a late hour. About 7.30 on Friday evening he went to Boydell's tailor's then and remained , hiding in the hack plice until the workmen had gone. He then went into the shop and made a bed for himself on Some it. T, the morning at 8.30, an emplsye at the shop named Smith returned and found the boy as- -14,e0 there. He was kept till daylight and given some breakfast. On Saturday the child went about the town all day and slept under a market stall at night. Sunday morning arrived, he went out begging again and in the evening was found wandering about Scotland-road by P.C. Bell who took him to Mrs. Daly's lodging heuse, where he was kept that night and the following night. On Tuesday morning the Inspector visited defendant's house in Sankey Bridges, and found the other children in s deplorably dirty state. A woman with whom the defendant co-habited was in the house but she said she did not know whether the child was turned out or not. Witness thought the boy was grossly neglected and in- formed the Bench that they had the power to inflict a penalty of £25 or send defendant to gaol for SiK calendar months.—James Smith em- plose at Boydell's shoo deposed to ending the boy on Saturday morning asleep on some woollen olnth. He took him out and asked the child why he did not go home and was told by the boy that he was afraid to go home. The bly had often called at the shop for remains of food.—Patrick Bartley, jun., the boy in qiies- Don, was then brought forward and it was found that lie had neither shoes nor stockings and was only half dresqed. He corroborated what the Inspector had said, to being afraid to go home.—A son of defendant, work- ing and living in Warrington, said that his father and the woman he lived with,repoatedly neglected and turned the children out. It was stated that defendant has been brought up 10 or 11 times for not sending his children to school and the Chairman (Mr. John Fairclough) remarked that he was convinced that defendant habitually neglected his chil- dren. This was a had case, and defendant would have to go to gaol for two months' hard labour.

Owe, long ago, I was witness to a duel in California. The two men had been bosom friends, but had quarclled about (of course) a woman. Splendid fellows both— young, brainy, and ambitious. As they stood in a clear space among the pins trees near Sacramento, pale as lilies, steady as rocks, weapons in hand waiting for the word, the rising run Ehining athwart the line of vision, they presented a picture too often seen in 1856. The pistols cracked almost simultaneously. One man stood erect, evidently untouched ; other fell upon his back and lay str sight and still. Seconds, surgeons, and spectators nigh ed to his side. He was " all there,' mind as well as body. " No, don't disturb me," he said coolly to the doctor, " Im shot fatally and shall die in five minutes, Call Jack and be quick." Pistol still in hand, his •antagonist came and bent over his ' erstwhile chum. Th.e excitement among the crowd was intense ; the dying man alone was calm. "Jack my darling old bny:" be said, " forgive vie and forgive her. Kiss me and let me go." A minute more and he was dead, with Jack lying acrcss his body, crying like a baby.

"My appetite w as variable; sometimes I could eat anything and again I could not touch any food at all. Bat I was raver laid up, as it were."
- , Please note the last sentence. It may seem like the weakest but really is the strongest point in this lady's statement. We will tell you why in a moment.

_ She goes on: " Still I was often in misery, but got along fairly well until August, 1890, when I had a severe attack of rheum& tier,. First the great toe of my right toot and the th urnb of my right heed grew hot and painful. lifter a time the trouble extended to my back and bins. I could not straighten myself; I was almost bent double. Month 'after month I was like this, get- ting little or no -sleep at night. Medical treatment proved of no benefit to me. In December, 1891, the pain almost drove me mad. My face was swollen to nearly twice its natural size, and my eyes were so cov- ered by the enlarged lids that I could scarcely see. There was a constant ringing in my ears, and the doctors said I had erysipelas. "For days and days 1 could not walk across the floor, and for some time I was able to move about only by taking hold of the furniture or other ottects. When all other means had been tried and had failed Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup -was recommended to me. A single bottle did me a deal of good. I kept on with it, and soon was,atrcager and in better health than for forty years previously. I still take an occasional dose and continue in good health, notwithstanding my ' age (48) and the ' change of life.' I tell everyone what the Syrup has d.ne for me, and give you permission to publish what I have said. Yours truly (Sizned). (Mrs.) Misr Jess MILNES, 18, Walker's Buildings, Brewery Lane, Thornhill Lees, near Dewsbury.Yorkshire, October 12th. 1892." . .
Now for the lesson of both these incidents ; what is it ? This : that it is not people in desperate extremi-
ties who suffer mos. Pain is in proportion to the

resistance to disease. Those who surrender, who are in despair, who give up.lhave present punishment largely remitted. Dying persons are the most comfortable of all. Hopelessness and dissolution administer their own anodynes. Those who are not laid vp, who are ill, and yet work and struggle, need pity and help. This tidy was one, and to such Mother Seigel always proves a friend..

-- - JOHN II EY /MOD. —A book which is scarcely knewn te young people of the present day, but which was exceedingly popular jn the earlier part of the 19th century, has been issued by the above publisher. The authoress is Mite. Barbara Rofland, who, in her day, was a prime and deserved favour- ite with old and young. "The Young Crusoe " is 1 the title of the book, which deals in a simple, yet entertaining manner with the experiences of a boy named Charles Crusoe, who is cast on the : island of St. Paul, in the Indian Ocean. At the commencement the hero's father and a negro boy are with him on the " one black speck on a sea of silver," but, an unfortunate incident. causes the two latter to he rescued by foreign sailors and unable to explain that the boy Charles is left behind. After months, ot privations and hardships " our hero" is recovered from his painful position end restored "hale and hearty • to the midst of his sorrowing family. Throughout the story there runs a vein of sinceintv sni faith in the Divine Power which teaches the reader a lesson worthy of remembrance. Numerous illustrations and copious explanatory notes add, not only to the interest and attractiveness of the book, but render it a medium of instruction on various objects and matters per- taining- to the land end climate forming the ground-plot of Mrs. Hofland's work. CASSELL AND Co.—Noth'ng could give UP greater pleasure than to announce the appearance of what is undeniably "The people's life of William Ewan Gladstone." Innumerable volumes have been written on the life of our greatest statesman. but none have, considerina its cheapness, been produced equal to Messrs. Cassell's edition of the above. Not only is it comprehensive and clear, but the whole biography is written in a style light and readable, and one which forms en agreeable change to the prosaic statements of facts which have hitherto been so common. Among its salient features are the illustrations of scenes, places, ,etc., connected with the life of Mr. Gladstone at nine different periods in his life's 71istory.a5 well as one of Mrs. Gladstone and her son, Mr. Herbert Gladstone, M.P. Photo- graphs of other statesmen, and eminent men in all stations of life are interspersed with •Ghe others. The price of the hook is a Popular one, placing it within the reachof all, viz. Is. GEORGE NEWNES AND Co.—With the January number of the " Picture Magazine" a new volume is commenced. All the old features have been re- tained so that the interest and attractiveness are assured to those who are familiar with the varied end entertaining illustrations which the • Picture magazine " has always contained. This armor- tunity of obtaining a complete series of monthly megazines of art, fun portraiture, and autographs, should not be neglected by all desirous of possess- ing a hook which will never grow old hut rather increase in value as the years roll on.—Aceompany- ing the new year has come quite an enidemic of cheap book e contaimng photographic reproductions of famous places, things and faces. div.p: C NAL.
IMPORTANT COM` FRENCE.

It is well within the knowledge of our readers that so far. the Snip Canal Co., have failed to carry mt tneir legal obligations to the Corporation and the Traders of Warrington, and that for some time past the important questions involved have been of the subject of most serious consideration on the part the Rivers' Committee. On the one hand there has been a desire to avoid adding unduly to the enorm- ous difficulties of the Ship Canal,while at the same time great caution has been necessary to prevent anything being done or left undone, which might in the smallest degree prejudice the. interests of the town. Up to the present time the Corporation and the Traders of the Borough have acted in concert, and so far as the Rivers Committee is concerned we are perfectly assured that it is their desire and de- termination to maintain the "entente cordiale " with the Traders to the fullest possible extent, and to allow no action to be taken which will in any sense diminish the privileges or. jeopardise the rights of those for whom they EICL as Trustees. Under the Ship Canal Act of 1885, the Company are required to dredge a certain section of the River Mersey to a death of 8 feet at low water and to maintain the same so dredged,and this work should have been completed before the opening of the Canal for traffic, that is before Jan, Ist 1894. The Canal Co., however, found this to be.a wholly im- possible task, and they approached the Corporation for an extension of time, which request after due consultation and agreement with the Traders was sanctioned as up to July 31st, 1894. This period was by a second agreement, which was .again ap- proved of by the Traders, further extended to Oct. 1, 1894, in consideration of which the Company undertook to complete the entrance to the Canal from the River, via Walton Lock and to pay as "liquidated damages" the sum of £5O per day for every day after Oct. 1,1894,that the dredging of the SE t. channel remained incomplete.
- The section of the River previously referred tu is not yet dredged to the required depth ant " liqui- dated damages" to the amount of some £6,000 has accumulated and continues to accumulate. - •

----- The fact is that the Canal Co. have realised that this" dredging" is likely to be the most trouble- some, if not the most costly piece of work they have yet to accomplish, and in the present condi- tion of their finances it is not to be wondered at that they have again approached the Corporation • with a view of obtaining for a period of time to be mutually agreed upon, some modification of this great liability. With this object, a short time age, a deputation 'from the Ship Canal Company, including Mr. Bythell, Mr. Southern, Sir L. Williams, Mr. Rill (engineer to Manchester Corporation), and others waited upon the Rivers' Committee,then under the, chairmanship of Councillor R. T. Fairciough (who has since resigned and been succeeded in the posi- tion by the then Deputy-Chairman, Councillor fl. Roberts), and requested that for a period of two years the Canal Compaoy should be required to maintain the "dredging ' to a depth of six frz-t, only instead of eight feet,and as a" quid pro quo" they offered to deepen the bed of the old river at Wilderspool so as to make it available for " dock " purpeises for vessels up to 9ft. draught, and also to provide a " deep water lay-bye" near the Stag Bridge on the canal for ocean going vessels to dis- charge or receive cargo. These proposals neces- sarily required and have received the most careful consideration of the Rivers' Committee, and have prictieally occupied their almost undivided atten- tion up to the present time.

It was the unanimous opinion of the committee from the outset that the "quid pro quo "offered by the Ship Canal deputation was by no means adequate to the modification of their liabilities which they were seeking, and with a view to secur- ing the completest counter proposals to be adopted by the Rivers' Committee,each member of the com- mittee was requested to formulate his ideas on the subject in writing, and to submit them for discus- sion at subsequent meetings of the committee This suggestion has been very thoroughly carried out alter much deliberation, but before proceeding further in the negotiations with the Ship Canal

Company, following the precedent which had always hitherto been adopted, the Rivers Com- mittee sent copies of their " counter proposals " to the Chamber of Commerce, the Rivers' Protection Association, and Messrs. J, Faitclough and Sons, with a request that the parties named would give I them their :areful consideration and afterwards I attend a conference with the Rivers Committee so as to form if possible a basis of common agreement with the object of afterwards meeting the Directors of the Ship Canal in order to bring the matter to a eatisfactory settlement,if possible. During the time which has been occupied by the Rivers' Committee in deliberating upon this very important matter, it is quite obvious that it would have been most indiscreet to have prematurely dis- closed the various items which had not yet been adopted as the " countrt proposals of the Corpora- tion," and considerable amusement bus resulted from the very ill-timed and ill-natured criticisms which have been publicly fulminated by some anonymous writers in the local press, whose want of knowledge on the subject has been equalled by their cool assumption of an authority which they certainly do not possess. In the meantime the Rivers Committee have obtained the opinion o f eminent counsel (Mr. Pembroke Stephens, Q.C.) upon their "case," and are gratified to know that their action is correct in every particular.

The Conference whicn was so summoned was held on Monday afternoon last at 2.30 o'clock in the Council Chamber at the Town Hall.under the pre- sidency of Coun.H.Rob,rts (chairman of the Rivers' Committee) and there vere present in addition, the Mayor (Couucillor James Fairclough) the Town Clerk, Borough Surveyor. Messrs. John Rylands„l. J, Ble.ckly, Carson, J. White, H. Greenall. J. C. Ridg- way, J. J. Crossfield representing the Rivers' Protec- tion Association ' • F. Monks, R. Garnett, Hutchings, repre§enting the Chamber of Commerce, John and H. Fairclough, and Councillor R. Heaton, Alderman Prancomb, Alderman Sutton, and Alderman Hutchinson, Councillor F. W. Monks, Councillor A. Bennett, (the Rivers' Committee). The meeting lasted an hour and a half, and a full and frank dis- cussion of the various proposals of the Rivers' Com- mittee and the additional suggestions made by the Rivers' Protection Association and the Chamber of Commerce, took place. The whole of the proposals of the Rivers' Committee with one very slight and comparatively unimportant exception, practically received the unanimous approval of the conference Messrs. Fairclough and Sons through their repre- sentative S formally objected to any deviation from the terms of the Ship Canal Act of .1885, but this of course is only to be expected seeing that their action" against the "Ship Canal Company still remains suspended. The proposals of the Rivers' Protection Association and the Chamber of Com- merce were formally received by the Rivers' Com- mittee and will most probably be absorbed into the final proposals to be submitted by the Corporation to the Ship Canal Company. The counter proposals of:the Corporation in the main will probably be that so long as the Ship Canal Company fail to carry out the obligations devolved upon them by the Act of 1885 to the Cor- poration and Traders of Warrington,the latter shall have the right to use the Ship Canal from Eastham to Warrington, free of toll ; that the Ship Canal Company shall deepen the old river at Wilderspool sufficiently to allow vessels of 10 feet draught to enter to and from the Canal at all states of the tide and shall provide wharfage and warehouse accom- modation sufficient for the trade that may he developed in this locality; that the Canal Company shall provide the " deep water lay-bye" mentioned in their own proposals ; that the "liquidated damage" of ..£5O per day, up to the data of the new agreement, shall be "deposited," and shall revive and continue to accrue on any default on the part of the Canal Compsny in carrying out the new agreement, and some further but less important conditions which need not now be ref erred to. At the conclusion of the conference, throughout wl,ich the most cordial feeling was shown on all sides, Mr. John Rylands, addressing the Chairman, said that while they (the members of the Rivers' Preservation Association) had for some little time past been somewhat doubtful as to whether the Rivers' Committee were fully alive to the very important interests of the Traders of the town, he I was hound to say, from what he had learnt that I efternoon. that, that fear was entirely unnecessary, that the Itivers'Committee had acted throughout in a most praiseworthy and business-like manner,and he was quite sure that their interests were perfect ly in the hands of the Committee to which the Corporation had entrusted this most important business. A cordial vote of thanks to the Chairman on the proposition of Mr.ll.Fairclough, concluded the proceedings.

div.head: AT WARRIN GTON.
div.p: AT WARRIN GTON.

The newly-formed Sunday School Union in con nection with the Warrington Wesleyan circuit,held- a most interesting:meeting on Wedneeday,last week The reports of he "detectives" who were appointed to visit the variousschools unawares, created much Interest, and had there been time, no doubt a spirited di-cussim would have ensued. However, the time was limited, for the cennexional secretary to the Sunday School Uniop, Rev. R. Culley, was present to address the meeting. His speech was a very valuable one, for it sparkled from be- ginning to end with suggestions as to the manner in which to keep proper discipline in the schools. If the teachers present would " read, mark, learn, aud inwardly digest" the suggestions thrown out, Mr. Culley's visit will not have been in vain.

At the conference which was held on the Monday last week, be wen the Rivers Committee, local traders, members lof the Chamber of Commerce and representatives of the Ship t anal Company, some matters of the utmost importance to Warrington were under discus•ion. The Rivers Committee, of which Councillor Henry Roberts is the chairman, have kept a very vigilant eye on the interests of the town which are at stake in these negotiations with the Canal Company, and I believe it will be found in the en I that they have made a very good bargain.

Mr. J. C. Parr's handsome gift to the town of new Public flail which he is building in Palmyra Square will be warmly appreciated. There certainly could have been no more suitable gift at the pre- sent time. For a few years past, Warrington has been about as badly placed as it was possible to be in regard to accommodation for large public gatherings, and the new bull ling will,in the fullest sense of the term, meet a long-felt want. On the whole Warrington has not had much reason to complain of want of generosity on the part of, at all event, some of its wealthier inhabitants or neighbours, and it goes without saying that Mr. Parr's gift is not by any means the least in the list of benefaction that might be enumerated.

It is to be regretted that the contributions to the Infirmary on Hospital Sunday 1894, were con- siderably less than they were on the previous year No doubt the coal strike caused a censiderab Is de- crease ot itself, but there are still some ch ches and chapels which do not make a collection rthe Infirmary at all. This is an ora on which should be rectified. There could be no better display of " practical Christianity" than by helping the Infir- mary. Perhaps something is due to forgetfulness. aLd therefore the officials of the various religious lbodies would do well to remember that Hospital 'Sunday this year is on March 17th.

Looking impartially at the report presented by the Technical Institute secretary, at the annual prize distribution in the Museum Lectureroom on Monday evening, last week, there are several points which do not compare favourably with those of the first year. The first is the fact that the number of attendances (luring the past session is not as large as that of the first session in 1892. It may very reasonably be pointed out that as 1892 was the year in which a Technical Institute was first started in Warrington, the number of students was greater because of the novelty of the project. Still, there is a satis- factory increase in the number of students this ses- sion as compared with last, but then last session there was a falling off of no fewer than 115 as compared with 1892. On the whole there is still some justification for the remark of Mr. F. Monks that the young people of Warrington do not take full advantage of the splendid opportunties now offered them. MERLIN.

div.head: WATUUNGTON BAKER SURMONEa
div.p: A WATUUNGTON BAKER SURMONEa
THE SALE OF BREAD BY WEIGHT.
INTERESTING CASE.
X

On Friday morning, at the Borough Police Court, be- ' fore Alderman Harrison (chairman), Dr. Gorhall, and . Mr. S. Wright, John Toft, baker, Bridge-st., was sum- moned and charged, that on Friday, the 11th inst., in Warrington, he unlawfully sold two loaves, otherwise than by weight. The solicitor for the defence was Mr. F. R. Roberts, M.A., L.L.8., and for the prosecution Mr. J. Lyon Whittle (Town Clerk), appeared. Mr. Whittle said that on the 11th of January Mr. Place (inspector of weights and measures) instructed his as- sistants to go to Mr. Tuft's shop, and they employed a boy named Topham to go into the shop and ask for a 41b. loaf and a 21b. loaf. The lad went in and was served with the bread without its being weighed. Mr. Place had weighed the bread and found the 41b. loaf 3 ' drachms over-weight, and the 21b. loaf 2 ounces andl 3 drachms light. Mr. Toft, when spoken to about the offence, said the small loaf was not a 2ib. one but a2l. cob. Mr. Taft by this admitted an offence against the Act, because he could not sell bread as a 2d. cab, but he must sell by some fixed denomination of weight. Mr. Whittle applied for the full penalty, because he said this was not Mr. Toft's first offence of this character.- -Andrew Topham (12), stated that on the 11th of the present month on the instruction of Mr. Place and Mr Newall, he went into Mr. Toft's shop for a 21b. and a 41b. loaf, and he was supplied with the bread by the assistant without its being weig led. He paid 21. for the 21h. loaf, and took both loaves to Mr. Place. Outside the shop there were Nr. Newall (assistant to Mr. Place) and Mr. Tooliam, his father. Cross-examined by Mr. Roberts, witite3s said that he paid 20. for the small loaf and 41. for the larger. He denied that the assistant who served him mentioned anything about the loaf being under weight. He had not asked her to weigh the loaf.—Mr. Newell, assistant market inspector, said that on the clay in question he was standing outside Mr. Toft's shop when the boy was sent in and ;se saw everything that took place. Neither of the loaves was weighed. After the bread was served he west into the shop and demanded the assistant's name and address. After some hesitation she gave it him. When questioned she sad "We do not sell 2lb I.,aves but 23. loaves," which were below 21bin weight. This, on the instructions of Mr. Vitt, she always told to customers who aaked for a 2lbloaf.—Crass-examintsdbv Mr. Roberts, witness admitted that he could not hear anything that was said when the transaction took place. —Mr. Topham, senior, caretaker of the market, corro- borated. Mr. Roberts contended that it was not necessary, that the bread should be weighed in the presence of the customer. The assistant was not asked to weigh the bread and his (Mr. Roberts') instructions were that his client had never refused to weigh bread in the presence of the customer, when asked, but on the contrary he was quite willing to do so. He drew attention to a case which was decided some years ago before Lord Justiee Colburn who shad said "tinder the circumstances of the case we do not think the baker was bound to weigh the bread in the presence of the customer but he was bound to weigh the bread at some time before, sale unless it was fancy bread." Mr. Roberts, maintained that his client did sell his bread by w-eight and that his customers have always know that what they bought was not a 21b loaf hut a 2.1 loaf, which was really considerably in favour of the customer. People came iato the shop and asked for a 21b loaf and lie understood that the price was 2±l. for that quantity of bread,and it was to do away with the difficulty of farth- ings that his client had decided to make a loaf wcighing • less than 21bs and inform his customers that it was sold at2d. Mr. Roberts cited two cases heard before sti- pendiary magistrates which were similar to this, arid the decisione showed that there was at least a discre- tion in the matter and he asked the bench to exercise that discretion. He contended that his client's customers understood all about the loaves from the outset when the difficulty about farthings arose about three months agii,owitig to a Change in the prices of bread. The mere fact that the bread was under weight was not sufficient evidence that the bread had not been weighed. His instructions were that the bread was always weighed in the bakehouse after hsking. There was, he said, no suggestion of fraud, and his client was more interested about his reputation as an honest and fair tradesman than by that trumpery charge. lie had only committed a technical offence against an old fashioned law. Ada Mary Rawling, stated that she had worked for Mr. Toft for five months. She remembered the boy Topham coming into the shop on the day in question. He asked for a 41b. loaf and she understood a 21. loaf She made no remark when she offered the loaves to tbe. boy, ashe did not think it necessary. When the cus- tomers came in fora 21h. loaf they were informed of the circumstances of the loaf being under 2tla, and of it being sold as aM. cob. It was the invariable rule to weigh the bread in the bakehouse, but she had never witnessed it,

The Chairman of the Berich said that there Was no doubt Mr. Tort had broken the 'law technically, but they were certain he had no fraudulent intention in doing 80. It was a purely technical offence. but they were compelled to deal with it according to law. Mr. Toft expressed his willingness to make 2-11 b, ; loaves for 21d., according to a suggestion of the Town Clerk. The magistrates eventualli 'decided to impoie a penalty of 20s: and costs.

THREE has been no lack of poli- TharnePpealiigtine.al c tieal pabulum during the last few days. Several prominent mem- bers of the Government, including the PRIME MINISTER, the CHANCELLOR Of the EXCHEQUER, and Mr. ASQUITH, have within a week delivered notable addresses to large gatherings of Liberals. The PRIME MINISTER had a splendid audience in Cardiff on Friday night when he outlined the pro- gramme of the Government for the session of Parliament that will soon be opened. It is evid- ent from the proceedings at Cardiff during the sittings of the National Liberal Federation, and from the vast concourse which assembled to hear Lord ROSEBEBY that in Wales at all events there is no falling off of Liberal enthusiasm. The number of- Tories who are returned for Welsh constituencies is not far from the vanishing poiht, and there is little reason to fear that they will be any more numerous after the nest general election. The sturdy Liberalism of Wales is united upon the question of disestablishing the. Welsh Church, and in plac- ing that measure in the forefront of the Liberal programme, Lord ROSEBERY roused a political ardour which is bound to produce good , results. The plea for unity amongst his followers which Lord Rosanzavathought it necessary to make should not pass unheeded. Is he pointed out, the difficulty of the Liberals and the Tories with regard to their programmes is of an entirely different nature. That of the Liberals is to keep the list of reforms which they think it necessary to effect within practicable. proportions; that of the Tories is te find some- thing out of which they can make a presentable programme of ar.y kind. The result is that while the dull dead monotony of Toryism is ruffled with no schisms,Liberals are apt to have their differences as to which measure should have priority. Under such circumstances there is only one safe course to pursue, and that is to entrust thee selection of measures to the Government who are the respon- sible heads of the party. ,

In his speech at Hull on Tuesday, Mr. Asckurrn brushed aside with a vigorous hand the cobwebs which some super-subtle dialecticians have woven around the question of the House of Lords. It haa been asked, how can Liberals who are divided amongst themselves as to whether the House of Lords should be "mended or ended," act unitedly upon any proposal to reform the heredi- tary Chamber? But, as Mr. Anntru pointed eut, these differences do not coma in at the present time. The Government do not propose to pull down an old constitution and build an entirely new one upon its ruins. The question before them is not whether there sh a be one or two Chambers, but, given two Chamber, what are to be their relations 'to one another, and towards the people of Great Britain. This being the question the Government proposes to deal with it in a straightforward and logical way. They propose that the House of Commons—the elected Chain- bar—shall be made supreme, and that the House of Lords, which is not elected and which is com- posed entirely of one class of the community, shall be deprived of its veto upon legislation. That is a clear proposition to make, and Liberals of any shade of opinion, whether they be "enders " or "menders,' can consistently combine in attempt- ing to give it effect. The subject of the entire abolitioit of hereditary legislators is still left for future consideration, though once the Lords have been deprived of their veto and their proceedings turned into a harmless masquerade the need for abolition will not be so pressing. SirWirmax HAROOIIRT met with little less than a royal reception from his constituents of Derby on Tuesday and Wednesday. On Tuesday in travelling to the Midlands he was met by several enthusiastic: crowds of Liberals at the railway stations at which he stopped, and at Derby he was escorted to his hotel by a torchlight procession On Wednesday he addressed a crowded meeting of his constituents in wkich there does not seem to have been a dissentient voice. subjects which, in his ease,were of special interest. One of these was that of the imaginary dissensions in the Cabinet, and the other; that of temperance reform. With regard to the first of these subject he was particularly emphatic. "T sometimes wonder," he said, " what class of man it is who de- liberately sits down to write that which be knows to be false, to serve the purpose of a party and to injure a political opponent. No doubt these creatures should be treated with the contempt they deserve but it is a profession which is discreditable, I think, in itself. These fables of dissensions in the Cabinet are the mendacious inventions of minds of the baser sort." This emphatic declaration will, we should think, nail the particular political counter- feat to which it relates to the counter. On the subject of temperance reform Sir Wirmem is as pronounced as ever. There is to be no playing false on this question. The Government adhere to their local veto policy,though they are prepared to alter their Bill sas to include the option of reducing the number of public-houses as well as of prohibiting them entirely. As Sir WM. Eliseo-yam contends there can be no objection on principle to this enlargement of the scope of the Bill, while. it may secure for it additional support.

WALES has been prominent this, Reminiscences Parliament.of • • week in the political world, anp not the least important and ix- teresting figure at the Cardiff conference oft he National Liberal Federation was that of Sir GEORGE OSBORNE MORGAN. Sir GEORGE has been described as the "Old Parliamentary Rand" of the Welsh party, and his six-and-twenty years at St. Stephen's certainly give him some claim to the title, though that is not a long period com- pared with the Parlianientary activities of such very," old hands as, saqMr. GLADSTONE or Mr. VILLIERS. It is long enough, however, for a man with open eyes and receptive mind to gather in- teresting experiences and form reliable opinions, and some of these the member for East Denbigh- shire has been retailing to an interviewer. In spite of a recent lamentable incident, he is of opinion that the House of Commons is a much more decorous assembly than it used to he; and, if we may judge from the story told him by an aged gentleman long since dead, about the great Prime Minister, PITT, there is good ground for the belief. The gentleman in question was once dining with a party of which PITT was a member when word was sent that the Premier was needed ; in the House of Commons. PITT had just finished his second bottle of port, and was so overcome that he had to grope his way to the door, but once in the House he made what was esteemed his greatest speech. John BRIGHT made two observations upon the story when it was told him by Sir George OSBORNE Moitahar—first, that there were no reporters in those days, and second, that everybody who did hear PITT had probably had, not two bottles of port only, but three. There was un- doubted acuteness in these observations. It is certain that a Prime Minister who, in these days, attempted to make a great speech in the House of Commons under such circumstances would not achieve a success. Even with regard to obstruc- tion it is questionable whether the House shows any signs of retrogression,for,after all,in these lat- er days we have had nothiug to compare with the achievement of Mr. VrircErtr SCULLY to which Sir GEORGE MonGAN refers. Mr. SCULLY WaS champion obstructive, on one occasion at least. He commenced to speak at a quarter past twelve, immediately after the House met, and he spoke till a quarter to six. At a quarter to six he • turned to the Speaker and said, " And now with these few preliminary illustrations, I shall address myself to the question before the House." Fortunately, the other members were relieved of the infliction by the adjournment at six, but the obstructionist had accomplished his task of talking out time. With regard to speeches that have had an effect on divisions in the House within his own experience, Sir Geonan gives the first place to JOHN BRIGHT'S address on the second reading of the Burials (Amendment) Bill, in 1875. " Its effect," he tells us," was quite remarkable; it is the greatest oration I ever heard ita the House, and the description of the Quaker funeral in it is, to my mind, one of the finest things in the English language." Full credit is given to Disraeli for his abilities as a Par- mentary tactician, and the adroit manner in which he parried an attack. We are told that in one instance a gentleman' who now sits elsewhere than in the House, had called the Irish party a disreputable crew.' 'What would the Prime Minister say,' Mr. ALIMANDEB Strnravarr demanded with natural passionj 'if I were to call him and his Cabinet a disre- putable crew ? ' DISRAELI got up with tin bland answer, Sir, I should take no notice of it whatsoever.' What effect that had on the Rouse," anybody who knows it will readily understand." Another incident which is related in this inter- esting interview relates to the misreporting ol members of Parliamentary. On one oceasion thl Ladies' Gallery was the question under discussion and one member remarked that the Gallery di4 not exist in the last century. Mr. BenEsrow Hon; commented upon this,that there were man: things in the last century at which the Hone winked. The way in which the papers put it nex morning, however, was "that there were triarb things in the Ladies' Gallery at which tha Mine winked." There was clearly a difference her between the words spoken and the words printed which was hardly fair to either the honourabl members or to tbe occupants of the Gallery. Ther is a pathetic interest at the present time in tin feet that Sir Geortok °swami MORGAN clasee PARNELL and Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL of the greatest Parliamentarians of his Cm. PARNELL was, he thought, a bort: king amort men. "It took him a long time to attain to ha position in the, Heitse ; but it was an altogethr unique position. He was an illustration of wilt a strong personality could accomplish in the Hoop of Commons.' When he used to get up to spei one could hear a pin drop, so earnest was lid attention."

ST. PAUL'S BIBLE CLASS, RUNCORN. A meeting of this class was held on Sunday after- noon, when there was a fair attendance. The President (Mr. B. Kniveton) gave a bible lesson,and answered questions asked by several members. A sacred solo was sung by Mr. John Leath wood, and Mr. William Cooke gave a recital on the organ. SUDDEN DEATH AT RUNCORN. _ .

An inquest was held at Runcorn Police Station, on Tuesday, by Mr. J. E. Worsley, relative to the death of Albert, six weeks' old infant of Mr. Mott- ershead.s7, Sewell-street. The child was found dead in bed by his mother about six o'clock on Sunday morning. The evidence of Dr. Robinson was to the effect that the child had suffered from congenital dropsy and that was the cause of death. A verdict in accordance with the medical testimony was returned.

div.head: SUPPER TO CABMEN AT RUNCORN.
div.p: SUPPER TO CABMEN AT RUNCORN.

On Tuesday evening, the first annual re-union of the Runcorn cabmen, took place at the London and North-Western Hotel, Lowlands-road. A substan- tial supper was provided, and efficiently served by Mr. and Mrs. Jones. Mr. H. Horton presided. Several toasts were honoured, songs being interspersed by the following: Messrs. Kay, Walter Yarwood, H. Booth, J. Henry Lee and S. Brereton. A hearty vote of thanks was tendered to the host and hoitess and the gathering concluded with the singing of the National Anthem. RUNCORN LIBBRA.L CLUB.

A meeting w—t-s held at the Liberal Club on Wed- nesday evening for the purpose of receiving nomin- ations for the various officeri of the club. The following nominations were sent in : President, Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., vice-presidents, Messrs. G. Bellamy, T. Dean, T. Lea. P. Speakman, S. Taylor, A. R. Norman, W. Ockleston and R. H. Posuett ; treasurer, Mr. W. Ockleston ; secretary, Mr. A Riley. Twenty gentlemen were nominated for the committee, but as only 13 are required a ballot will have to be taken at the annual meeting of mem- bers to be helGI next week. BETHESDA LITERARY AND SOCIAL CLASS.

A meeting in connection with the above-named class waa held on Tuesday evening in the Lecture- room. Being an "open night" a paper by one of the lady members was read and then criticised by the Rev. T. Simpson. The paper was a very good one, and displayed thought and much tact in the synthetical manner in which the subject in hand was treated. After the criticism the paper was left for open discussion by the members. ELECTIONS IN RUNCORN DISTRICT.

At Whitley, on Saturday, a poll was taken for a rural district councillor. On the last occasion there was a tie between Messrs. Mounfleld and Rumney. The same candidates again went to the roll. Tne booth was at the Church Sunday School, and Mr. F. Johnson was the presiding officer. Soon after 8 o'clock this gentleman announced the result of the voting, namely, Mountield 22, Rumney 14. One vote was spoiled. An election for the ninth in“m- ber of the Parish Council at Norley took place on Saturday, and resulted as follows :—Mr. William Thompson, 43; Mr. G. Edge,3B. The polling booth was at the National RChclql, and Nit.. Gorge Ashton was the presiding officer. SEAMEN'S INSTITUTE, RUNCORN.

Mr. Shaw, missionary, presided at the weekly entertainment, provided at the above-mentioned institute on Tuesday evening. There was a good attendance. A miscellaneous programme of songs, recitations, etc., was well gone through. Ttie soloists were Mrs. R. Shaw, Miss Randles, Miss Shallcross, Mr. Cliff, Mr. Shallcross, Mr. Moores,Mr. Price, and Mr. T. Shaw. A Lancashire reading was given by Mr. A. Waterworth, and Miss E. Marshall contributed a recitation. Mr. Jahn Foulkes per- formed a pianoforte solo. The accompanists were Mr. A. Price and Mr. J. Foulkes. A pleasant even- ing was spent.
