In Bethesda schoolroom, on Friday evening,about 100 members and friends of the Runcorn Musical Society were present at a ~ocial gathering. Mr. J. Brundrit, J.P., president of the society, gave a brief address, in which he spoke words of advice to the members. The hall was tastefully dE corated for the occasion by Mr. Leach, jun., and Mr. D. Lea. A programme of dances was gone through, the music being supplied by the society's orchestra, under the leadersl.ip of Mr. IL Pierpoint. Mr. James Booth satisfac.orily fulfilled the duties of M.C. Dur- ing the evening songs were given by Messrs. Bir- kett, Mason, Scott, Percy Jones, and Jos. Littler. Light refreshments were partaken of during the evening. Tins RECENT SICK NURSING EXAMINATION.

The result of the examination in sick nursing (second course) has been received. Of the 18 can- didates who sat for examination, 16 have passed and two failed. Three candidates passed with dis- tinction and obtained a prize. The following are the results with the number of marks obtained. 145 marks and over gain a certificate and prize, and 112 marks and over receive a certificate. The highest nun ber of marks obtainable was 160. Mrs. W. H. Once, 150; Miss A. M. Mack, 150: Mrs. Harrop, 145; Mrs. S. A. Davies. 140; Mrs. Parkinson, 140:. Miss C. Withington, 140; Miss M. A. Smith, 140: Nfrs. J. P. Rillcross, 135 ; Miss M. E. Wilton, 135 • Mrs. James Littler, 130; Miss B. Rowland, 130; Mrs. T. Whinyates, 127; Mrs. M. E. Norman, 127; Mrs. W. Matthews, 125; and Mrs. I', Le Couteur, 122. FORRION MISSIONARY MARTINO AT Rumconrw. _ . _

A meeting under the auspices of the Church of England Society for the propogation of the Gospel was held in the National schoolroom, Church-et., on Tuesday evening. There was a large attendance. In the absence of the Vicar (Rev. Canon Wood) the chair was occupied by the Rev. J. Holden. The Chairman said he would like to put before them the following statement to show what was being done in Runcorn, especially at All Saints, for the " S.P.G." They had collected £26 124. flid. by means of those useful little collecting boxes ; .£8 Ils. 81. in subscriptions : end collections in the churches amounted to £l5 15s. 23/4d., which together with what they generally got at meetings like the present brought the total amount to about £57. That was the largest amount they had collected for the society. except in one year when they had a -donation of £5 He then called upon Archdeacon Shearq,who gave an interesting address on the work of the Society, especially in the colonies. The lecture was illustrated with views by the aid of a lantern. CONING OP AOR RRIoICINGS AT RUNCORN.

About eighty guests assembled at the Seamen's Institute on Friday evening in response to the in- vitations of Mr. and Mrs. Abel, of Tower House, Greenwsv-road, to celebrate the coming of age of their son Fred. Mr. F. 'Wilma!' presided over the Proceedings. After partaking of dinner a number of toasts were honoured. Those of a loyal and patriotic character were submitted by the chair- man. The health of the host and hostess was pro- posed Ly Mr. James Littler, who referred to Mr. and Mrs. Abel being alwsys ready with their purse to help forward good works and to assist the poor in the time of need. Mr. Abel, in responding,thank- ed these present for the enthusiastic manner in which they had drunk the health of himself and wife. Mr. A. Abel also responded to the toast. `• The Visitors" was next proposed by Mr. Hewitt, of Top Locks. Mr. Taylor, of Southport, responded to the toast. Mr. li. Annett next proposed the toast of the evening, that of the health of Mr. Fred-Abel which was suitably acknowledged. The last item, on the toast list was tent of the health of Mr. W. Shaw, which was proposed by Mr. A. Abel. 'lbis ' was duly responded to. An enjoyable evening was afterwards spent, various games being indulgsd in, and several songs Rung. The isied persona and poor children's treat com- mittee met at the Town Hall, Runcorn, on Monday evening, to take into consideration the advisability or otherwise of holding the treats this year. Mr. !raison. J.P.. occupied the chair, and there were also present: Revs. H. B. Firth, J. Holden, Dr. McKenzie. Messrs. J. D. Jones, T. Cooke, and Mill- ington (scrstariss); g. Taylor. J.P., R. IT. Posoett, M. J. Sweetmen. J. Robinson, T. Bowyer, T. Williams, W. Crosby, T. Reynehis, 11. Wright, T. Wocrl. Coventry, J. s. Smith, Wm. Shaw, W. Dudley, 143. Key, .1. F'. Moulton and G. Howard. Mr. Taos, Cooke read the balance sheet of last year's treats, showing that the aged person's treat coat in in^n.v .£ )11 24. 51.. and the treat to tytor children. £2l' lAs. ; leaving a balance at the bankers of £2.3 104. I. Namerons gifts of goods were received In addition to the subscriptions. The feelingof the meeting was that a trent to the aged firsons should b 4 given provided it could he done without appeal- ing to shoolcsspers or those who ware contributing to rhs fund, and that the ohildren's treat shonld be postponed until a more fatronrable oppor- tunity occurred, A sub-committee consisting of %isssrs. I. !raison, S. Tat lot, J. Robinson, R. 11. Posnott, W. Shaw. and J. B. llolland.was appointed Qre whether it would be possible to raise an additional amount to that already in hand without arpealing to those people who are already contri- buting to the relief funds. and to report to:the next meeting of the committee, la by held on Mjnday
DRUNKENNESS.

At Runcorn Police Court on Thursday morning, before Mr. Thos. Handley, Patrick Whelan, was fined ss. and costs, or in default of payment, seven days' imprisonment, for being drunk in Public Hall-street, Runcorn, the previous night. HALTON-ROLD WIt4LAYAN CHOIR, RUNCORN. . . . .

At the annual meeting of this choir, on Tuesday evening, which was held in the church. the follow- ing appointments were made:—Mr. Johnson, re- elected choirmaster ; Mr. Welsby, secretary ; Mr. Wm. Wickstead, treasurer ; and Mr. Wm. Leath- wood, librarian. Mu. BRUNNKR, M.P., AND TEIS NORTIIWICH

div.head: EX &MINER SATURDAY, JANUARY 26, 1895.
div.p: THE EX &MINER SATURDAY, JANUARY 26, 1895.
GUARDIANS.

Mr. Brunner, M.P., has declined the offer of the Nort hwich Board of Guardians to be elected a mem- ber under the new Act of Parliament,on the ground that his Parliamentary duties keep him away a full half of the year, and especially in the hope that his action might result in the restoration of another gentleman whom he named to the membership. SHOOTING- ACCIDENT NEAR RUNCORN. On Weylnesday afternoon, a Liverpool gentleman, whilst out shooting on the estate of Mr. Wade, at Aston Grange near Runcorn, was accidently shot in the hip. Medical assistance was immediately sought for, a messenger being despatched to Frodsham on horseback. Drs. Selly and Burton, of that town, were soon in attendance and found that the gentle- man's wound was of a serious nature. NARROW ESCAPE FROM DROWNING. Mr. Thomas Tullock, piermaster of the Bridge- water lock, Runcorn, had a narrow escape from drowning on Wednesday night. In the darkness, he fell into the lock, at the time when the steamer Ellen, which was towing several flats, was coming through. A line was thrown to him, and he suc- ceeded in placing his arm into the noose, and was drawn out of the lock at a moment when he was in imminent danger of being crushed, between one of the vessels and the stonework, lie was, however, little the worse for the immersion on Thursday. THE RUNCORN VOLUNTEER BAND. A social gati.ering of members of the Volunteer Rand at Runcorn, and their friends, was held on Wednesday evening at Mr. A. Riley's café. A tea was provided, and the subsequent proceedings were presided over by Bandmaster Outhwaite. Speeches were delivered, and Mr. Moorfield gave a cordial welcome to Sergeant Callagan whe succeeds Sergt., Instructor Player,. that officer having retired on a pension. A vote of thanks was accorded Sergeant Player for the services he had rendered to the band. A programme of vocal and instrumental music was gone through during the evening. Songs were contributed by Messrs. Parry, Evans, G. Garratt, Shaw, W. and A. Outhwaite. A solo on the mandoline was given by Mr. Smith and Mr. F. Pepe played a concertina solo. Mr. W. G. Mr. T. Simister presided over the procoedings, which were of a most interesting character. DR ATE OP MRS. LB COUTEUR. About ten o'clock on Tuesday morning, Sarah Le Couteur, wife of Captain J. Le Couteur, of 26, Trentha m-street, Runcorn, died after an illness extending over nearly three months, at the age of 62 years. She was the daughter of the late Mr. John Anderton, shipbuilder, Castle Rock-yard, Run- corn, and therefore belonged to one of the oldest Runcorn families. She was married about 40 years ago to Captain Le Couteur, and worshipped at Bethesda Congregational Church. She had ben ailing about ten weeks when she sustained a slight atroke, and this was followed by one of greater severity, and from the shock sustained by the sudden disappearance of her son, Frederick John—who is still missing—she has never rallied. Dr. Mangan has been in constant attendance. The cause of death was paralysis. She was well-known and highly respected in the town, and much sympathy is extended to the bereaved ones. The funeral will take place on Saturday at Runcorn Cemetery. RuNconN TECHNICAL iNBTITVYA.

BY OUR RUNCORN CORRESPONDNNT.

There is still but a gloomy outlook for an early revival in the chemical trade. In fact, the letter of Mr. Morrison, a summary of which was given last week in the " Examiner," tends to deepen the gloom. The men who were engaged at the works, be said, shonld be recommended to seek work else- where, as there was no immediate prospect of the chemical works getting into full swing again. But thisps almost as bad as to tell the men to take coals to Newcastle, for there is a general depression of trade throughout the conntry,and large numbers ot " unemployed "are to be tound in every town. The question arises is it impossible to find them wlrk of some kind in the towril We have heard a great deal for some time now, about the provn of a graving dock at Runcorn, of counter proposals,and alternative proposals, and that is where the matter still stands.

But the members of the new Urban Council are moving in the matter, and at the meeting on Tues- day of the Parliamentary and General Purposes Committee, it was decided to ascertain the views of representatives of the trades' societies and repre- sentative unions on the subject. These will meet the committee next week, after which it is to be hoped the committee will lose no time in formula- ting their proposals on the matter, which aro ulti- mately to be submitted to the Manchester Ship Canal Company for their approval. Apart from the benefit Runcorn will, or ought, to derive from such a provision, the construction of the graving dock or lay-by would be the Means of finding work for numbers of men in the town at present without employment, and who are unable to obtain any. But our local parliament has been slow in dealing with the matter, and perhaps the Ship Canal Co. will be still slower.

What next ! A " shoe black " brigade is shortly to be commenced in Runcorn. Already the clothes for the youths and the materials required have been bbtained, and soon a brigade of six youths will be at work, or to be more strictly correct— ready for work. In addition to being open to "shine your boots " they will be at liberty to carry messages or parcels. The movement is the outcome of the recent prosecutions of youths for touting at the railway station, and Mr. Shaw, mis- sionary, has started the brigade in the hope of find- ing them a little better employment. Whether Runcorn is large enough to find work for such a brigade remains to be seen.

'To be or not to be hot lunch er a cold lunch. That was the question which the members of the Runcorn Board of Guardians had to set themselves to decide at their meeting at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday afternoon. The matter re- lates to the lunch which the members have been able to have at the Workhouse on Board days. It has previously been supplied hot, but the number of diners has largely increased of late, with the result that if the hot lunch is to be provided, fur- ther accommodation would be required, and in all probability a cook would be necessary. As an alternative, to avoid this additional expense, the dining committee recommended that a cold lunch only should be supplied for the same charge as pre- viously, viz., one sniffing. By this means the lunch could be left on the table an hour and a half,whick would prevent the members having all to dine at one sitting, and turther dispense with a great deal of cooking. But this suggestion did not meet with the unanimous approval of the members some of whom did not like the idea of paying a shilling for a cold lunch. The matter had to be put to the vote, but the committee's recommendations were carried by a small majority. The Trades' Hall at Runcorn is now being used by the whole of the Trades Societies in the town for the purpose of holding,their meetings in. But the Friendly Societies have not come forward with the same unanimity. Several of them, however, intend to make the hall their headquarters, and if they are wise, the other societies will follow suit. The hall has been expressly built for the purpose, and is, surely, preferable to the dingy "pub." The more numerous the societies that make use of the hall the less will be the charge to each for main- tenance.

div.head: DEATH OF LORD RANDOLPH. CHURCHILL.
div.p: DEATH OF LORD RANDOLPH. CHURCHILL.
It is with regret that we announce ths death of Lord Randolph ChurChill, which took place at a quarter-past six o'clock. on Thursday morning at his residence in Grosvenor-square, London. . . .

The following bulletin was issued on Thursday mern- ing at 4.15 a.m. :—"Lord Randolph Churchill passed away peacefully and without pain at 0.15 this morning. --(signed) Ronson Room. M.D.: G. E. KEITH, M.R. Viscount Curzon desires it to be stated that Lady Randolph Churchill, the Dowager Duchess oi Marl- borough, and the other members of the family won present at the bedside. The funeral will be on Monday, and it is understood that thy interment will take plsee at Bladon Church, near Blenheim. Dr. Moose states that the end came after some thirty hours of unconsciousness, and was naturally painless and peaceful. It is understood that the latter part of the fight against death was ono of the most remarkable that has been known in the experience of the medical attendants. Lord Randolph had been for some time in a moribund state. When the members of his family were summoned to his bedside last evening his pulse was so feeble as to have practically ceased, and the end was momentarily expected when the pulse suddenly improved and he was considered far less near an immediate dia. solution than for some time previously. The change, however, proved to be merely an expiring flicker. Lady Randolph Churchill and the Dowager Duchess of Marl- borough feel the blow very keenly. Telegrams anneuneinn the death were sent to this Queen. the Prince of Wales, the Duke and Duchess of Connaugh, the Czar of Russia, and the Emperor of Germany, and also to Lord Rosebery and other members of the Government.

Sunday was Choir Sunday at the above place of worship, when special services were preached on behalf ef tho choir. The Rev. D. W. Kirtlan explained that the collec- tions of the previous day, and the proceeds of the tea and lecture would go towards reducing the debt upon the Sunday school. He said that the debt at present amounted to about £250. They had to pay a ground rent of £l2 per annum, and altogether they had to pay something like £4O or £5O to keep the premises of the school and church open. He was grateful to those whe had responded to his solicitations to give some- thing towards the scheme, and he had scarcely had a refusal. The chairman expressed his pleasure at being present that evening. He said he was always willing to help them at Sankey Bridges. He was sure the lecture that evening would be an interesting one, because it was about an interestihg subject. (Laughter.) He then ealled upon Mr. Sellers to give his lecture.—The lecturer said that his subject was of interest to everyone. Women liked to hear about women, and he was sure the opposite sex did also. (Laughter.) The lecturer then went on to contract the state of women in former times with their present condi- tion. He next proceeded to speak of their virtues and failings, and concluded with an eloquent account cf the good work which is being done or which could be done by women in various stations of lit e.—The lecture was listened to with rapt attention, and at the close a hearts' vote of thanks was accorded to both Chairman and lecturer, on the motion of Mr. J. Summergill, seconded by Mr. W. Brough, the latter of whom stated that Mr. Parker had promised to make the takings of the anni- versary into £2O. The meeting was brought to a close in the usual manner.

div.head: SHIP CANAL. IDE NORTH GERMAN LLOYD LINE AND MANCHESTER.
div.p: SHIP CANAL. IDE NORTH GERMAN LLOYD LINE AND MANCHESTER.

The North German Lloyd Line Steamship Company are about to establish a direct service of cargo steamers between Manchester and Bremen. Four weeks hence the first vessel will probably arrive in the canal, and a few days later will sail for Bremen. The steamers to be employed will be of about 1.000 tons burden, and it is anticipated that there will be a full cargo available for each trip. At first the service will probably be monthly, but an increase in the sailings can be made as exigencies require. The Company have been led to take this step for economic reasons. At present they send from Lancashire large quantities of goods over the Lan- cashire and Yorkshire Railway te Hull to be forwarded by their own steamers to Bremen. By adopting Man- chester as their port for the trade of the district they will practically save and earn themselves the whole cost of railway transit, which is eery considerable. The new departure will involve but very slight rearrangement of the existing Nerviere ef the North German Lloyd.
A GENERAL CARGO FROM NEW YORK.

The-;te-a-Meßiela, from New York, which arrived in the docks late on Saturday, brought a general cargo of 1,700 tons, and affords a capital illustration of what may he called the domestic benefits the Ship Canal was to bring to the district, apart altogrther from e-nsa- , tional items as to cotton and other materials for staple industries. The premise with regard to food and general supplies has Aiwa). caught the public attention, and has been much encouraged by the table of com- parative savings, recently published by the Company, which ',tinge many articles of food into striking pro- minence. The Meta brought a large consignment of cheese far the Wholesale Co-operative Society ; 400 tons of lard for Messrs. Eileen and Sons, Limited (who have signified their intention to tiring the whole of their large iennorts direct to Manchester by canal) ; also shout 2,000 cases of tinged meats ter Messrs. Libby, M•Niel, and Libby,and 3218 bales, or 10,700 sides, of heavy sole leather for Mr.R.Proetor. Mr Troct.or state s that be had • little difficulty at first in fixing matters of detail, but this is hie second lot, and he is in lie groove now, and means to continue there, adding OW the advantages are •• decided." Manufacturers am' 'lidera can thus, by individual determination and •II 'o-operation,make up hundred, of :general cargoes, mud torm much more than th• nucleus of the desired Ship Canal revenue. A STEAMER STRANDED AT WESTON.

The anchor line st•amship " Britannia " was proceed- ing down the canal about two o'clock, en Wednesday afternoon, when she struck on the bank near Weston Mersoy lock. At the tune she struck she was drawing 20ft. forward and 2215. aft, and was assisted down the canal by toe tugs. She remained aground with her bow on the hank until tour o'clock, when, by the aid et additional tugs idle was swung stern round, and even- ually slipped off the bank. She then proceeded down 1,. canal to Saltport, where the pilot considered it wise sr bee to be tied up until Thursday morning, MISHAPS NEAR RUNCORN. •

On Thursday morning, the steamship Clan Fraser, whilst in her way towards Eastham, when reaching the sluices near Saltport ran aground. Cmsiderable time elapsed before she was got off the bank.—The steamship Lougbrigg tiolme, containing cotton on approaching the bend of the rand l near Runcorn bridge, struck the bank an Thursday morning. The. tug which was assisting her ,succeeded in pulling her off.
ENTERTAINMENT AT THE TRADES' HALL, RuNco RN. _ _

On Monday evening there was a crowded atten- dance in the Trades' Hall, John-st., Runcorn, to witness an entertainment provided by a local troupe of amateur minstrels. The proceeds were in aid of the local distress fund. The programme was of a miscellaneous character, and consisted of songs and choruses, a stump speech, quartette,mandoline solo, and cornet solo given by tte following Messrs. W.Ceoper. B. Holt, J. Harvey. F. Bishop, W. Skillicorn, R. McGrath, J. Camnbell,R. Williams, T. Charleston, and F. W. Smith. The stump speech was given by one of the members of the troupe who assumed the cognomen of Pro. Longjaw. The entertainment concluded with the performance of • most laughable sketch. The accompaniments were played by a small instrumental bind. Mr. F. W. Smith was the musical director; Mr. B. Bolt, man- ager ; Mr. W. tikillicorn, secretary ; and Mr. J. Rathbone, treasurcr. Tne pianists were Mr. Le Couteur and Mr. A. Price.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
DUTPUTE ABOUT A DOG'

At the Borough Police Court,on Frida.y,before kilder- man Harrisvn, Dr.Gornall,Councillor Roberts and Mr.S. Wright, Joseph Skidmore, Longford-st., was charged with stealing on 7th January, a black and tan terrier bitch, value £3, the property of William Raybold, Win- wick-road. Mr. Arthur Browne appeared for defendant and Mr. Percy Davies for the complainant.—Mr. Davies said the complainant was Wm. !Raybold, 170, Winwick- road, and worked at Dallam Forge, the defendant Jos. Skidmore, was also employed at Dallam Forge. In Nov. 1893, the defendant gave to complainant a black and tan terrier bitch, and about two days after Christmas day 1893, the bitch was given by the defendant to the son of complainant, John Raybold, on the , condition that defendant was given a pup when any were born. The complainant kept the dog until last Monday week, and took out a Beefiee for the animal on the 3rd Februery. On Monday the 7th inst, the com- plainant was walking aleng Winwick-road with the bitch, and whilst passing Oliver-st., the defendant came out of a public-house whistled to the bitch which went to him, and defendant picked it up and ran away with it. Complainant followed, but was unable to catch de- fendant. He afterwards visited defendent's house but could not get the dog back.—Wm. Raybold, the com- plainant, corroberated, and John Raybold, living with his father, said the defendant gave him the biteh in question by al deed of gift which was witnessed and signed. The document contained the conditions mentioned. A document said to be the one was pro- duced in court, but witness denied the signature as his. HeWas asked to write his name and his ,writing was found to tally with that on the document, though be still denied it. Mr. Davies also acknowledged that the signatures were identical, and said it was useless going further with the case.—The complainant, father of the last witness, did not know anything about this docu- ment, but on the recommendation of his solicitor he asked to withdraw the case as he had taken out a sum- mons on the strength of what his son had told him. On this withdrawal Mr. Browne applied for the costs and was granted two guineas. Two 13F0 WHO IMPOSTERS. At the Borough Court on Saturday morning before Mr J. .Burgess (chairman) and Mr. S. Chandley, John Leonard and Isaac Dagnall, were charged with being idle and disorderly persons and with begging in Sankey! street at 7.10 on Friday evening. DS. Monaghan said that on Friday evenine, he received a complaint about the two defendants going round begging with a book and card. He saw them in town drunk and stopping people. The first defendant had received £1 is. id. in Warrington by stating that they were out of work and had wives and families starving in Wigan. They were really single men and " downright imposters" Evid- ence as to the defendants' begging was given by two witnesses and both men were sent to gaol for seven days hard labour. A THIEF SURPRISED BY A THIEF. At the Warr:lit:ton Borough Court on Tuesday, before Mr. E. J. Guest and Dr. T. Starkey Smith, William Higginson, a boatman, last from Liverpool, was also charged with stealing from the ehep of Edgar V. Morton fit. James-street, on the 19th inst., a man's overcoat, valued 163. The Chief Constable stated that at 615 on Saturday evening, Mr. Ashton, the manager of Mr. Morton's shop missed the overcoat, and he reported the matter- to the pollee. From information received D.S. Monaghan and P.C. Bell went to the house of ' a man named Taylor in Orford-street and found the prisoner there. He at once admitted taking the overcoat, and else took the officers to the shop of Mr. Dckson, Church-Street, where he had pawned it, under the name of Thomas Jones, captain of the boat Sarah Jane. He WAS then taken to the police station—Prieoner ipon being asked what he I bad to say,said Viet he did not take the overcoat off the nail. Upon turning the corner in St. James-street, he saw a man take the overcoat off the nail. but when the man saw him. he dropped. the coat and ran away. He (the prisoner) then picked it. up and put it on.—Mr. Guest said that shopkeepers hrld no rieht to hang over- coats in such a tempting fashion as they did. The prisoner would be sent to gaol for roe menth. AEOTHER THEFT FROM A SHOP DIrR. John Norris. St. Helens, was charged at the Warring- ton Borough Gant on Tuesday, with st,aling from the shop door of Baker and Sons. on Monday afternoon, four pairs of hoots valued 14a. Mr. Hunt said that at 1.5 p.m. on Monday ; prisoner was seen to snatch the hoots 'which were hanging at the door of Baker and Sons boot shop. Finding out that he had been seen, the pri- soner threw the boots up Castle-qt., and ran along Sankey-at. He was seen by Alice Pritchard to en int* the Queen's Hotel yard. Mr. Pritchard, who is the manager of the shop, followed him, and gave him into the hands of the police. When charged at the Police Station, the prisoner pleaded guilty to tailing the boots. —Mr. Pritchard, in reply to Dr. Smith. 'aid that the prisoner was drunk at the time, and had it not been that he had been so abusive, he would not have given hitn into the hands of the police. The bnots were eight feet from the ground, and prisoner could not get them withont snatching them.—Prisoner was sent to gaol for 'One month.

AN OLD OFFENCE. Thomas Cloynes was charged at theWarrinaton Police Court, on Tuesday, with stealing from the hiwelling- house af Peter Connolly. 8, Morris-eolirt. off Chnreh-st., a pair of boots, valued 54., or. January 22nd, 1893. It was stated by Mr. Hunt tha;:. Clovnes was a relative of Connolly. and had been staying dining the night of the abeve date in his house. At 530 am. he got up and went away, taking the compl iinant's boots with him. Neither the prisoner nor the boo's were seen again by the police, until Monday this week, when prisoner was met by D.S. Monaghan, who took him to the Police Station.—Connolly said that prisoner was his brother-in. law, and about six months after the theft had been com- mitted, he came to his house,and asked him to look over it. Witness forgave him, and he did not new wish te press the case acainst him lithe polies had not arrested the priconer,he would not have taken any action against hiM.—The magistrates committed prisoner to prison for one month.

Stafford was granted temporary authority, to sell intoxicants at the "Smith's Arms," Legh-st., in plane of Samuel Jones. SNOWBALLING IN, THE STREET.—ThOMai Fallon, Walsh's-yard, Lawrence Garretty, Bakehouse-yard ; John Knockton, 13, Old-road, were all charged with throwing snowballs in Wildersp )01-road, on the 13th January. AB pleaded not guilty.—P.C. Corbett stated that on the day named he received a complaint from two ladies about being snowballed by some lads in Wilderspool-road. He proceeded there and found the de- fendants snowballing an old man. They ran away, but from a boy named Campbell he ascertained their names. —Their parents not being willing to have them birched, each defendant was fined 2s. 6d. AN ALLEGED FEROCIOUS DOG.—Thomas Morrison, of Lyons-St., Latchford, employed as a labourer on the Ship Canal, made an application to the Bench to stay any proceedings that might be pending against him for allowing his dog—which was regarded as dangerous— to waneer at large without being mezzled. He in- formed their worships that he had the animal destroyed. —The Head Constable explained that the offence had been reported, and a summons would have been taken out against the man. It would appear that the dog had got loose on a certain occasion, and had bitten a little girl on the leg. Morrison had been previously warned that if another complaint was made about his dog, proeeedings would be taken against him. The magistrates wished to have evidence of the destruction of the dog, and this having been produced, they assent- ed to the application. WEnNasnar.-7Before Mr. John Fairclongh .(chairman),

Mr. J. Geddes And Mr. J. B. Fleming. EXTENSION or. Tisez.—Mr. Taylor was granted an ex tension of time on the occasion of the Infirmary Bal and Parish Church Dance,at the Lion Hotel, until 2 t. yn AN EIOHT YEAR OLD oEo:MGT.—William Duvo,. was charged with having run away from the Boroug' of Warrington on the 31st March, 1886, leaving two children chargable to the common fund of the Warring- ton Union.—Mr. B. Shearer. enquiry officer, prosecuted on behalf of the Warrington Guardians and stated that the prisoner's family were first given in charge in 1882, and they had remained cent nuously so until they were sent out for " service." Three times previ msly the prisoner had been convicted I r the same offence and in 1856 he left Warrington, and a warrant was issued for his arrest, hut it was, only this week that he was appre- hended. The total cost for maintaiding the two children has been £l7O. One went to "service "in 1887 and the other in 1890. The prisoner was committed to gaol for three months' hard labour Orr OF GAOL AND IN AGAM—Julia Ann Shields,was brsught up for the second time this year, on a charge of being drunk and disorderly in Dial-st., at 11 p.m. on Tuesday night. Sergeant Chantler proved ending the prisoner in the condition stated. Speaking Vs the Bench, the Magistrates' Clerk informed them that the prisoner had only been out of gaol one day from a similar offence. She was sent back to gaol for another 14 day's hard labour. THIIIISDAT.—Before Mr. S. Chandley and Alderman Sutton. AN UNNATURAL FATHER.—Robert Clark was charged with assaulting his daughter Mary Egen, on the 21st inst.—Mary Ellen Clark, complainant, stated that on Monday night when she came home her father was in bed drunk. He asked her for his tea, but could not have any as he had not been working, and they had no- thing to give him. He struck complainant on the face, and threatened to strike her mother for interfering. Defendant denied the charge, ARd attempted to blacken Isis daughter's character.—Mr. Hunt stated that both complainant and her mother bore good characters, while defendant was addicted to drink, and lazy.—The magistrates bound defendant over to keep the peace for three months in a surety of £s,or in default 14 days' bard labour. PRIZE DISTRIBUTION. The annual distribution of prizes, consisting of nice!) bound boeks,to the scholars attending St. John's Church Sunday Ochool, and the Mission Sehool, took place en Monday evening in St. John's Hall, Earlestown. Tnere was a very large audience. • Previou3 to the distribution, an operetta entitled " Princess 'tiny Tat," was performed by a number of the school children, who had been trained for the occasion by Mrs. Latimer. organist. The children sustained their parts in an admirable manner, which evidenced the careful training they had received. All the girls composing the chorus were arrayed in white, and a very charming picture they presented. When the curtain rises,Princess "Tiny 'rot " (Miss Emily Fluglius) is seen scared on a raised • dais. It is her birthday, and after reciting the intro- duction, " Mother Redcap " (Miss A. Clarke) appears, and promises to grant her anything she may wish. The Princess replies that she retains a " Major Henan " (Master Harry Toft) to make up her mind for her. The Major Domo handed to the Princess a book of nursery rhymes,from which she selects certain rhymes she would ' like to see represented. Thereupon, most of the well- known rhymes are illustrated, such as "Jack and Gill," " Mother Hubbard,"" Boy Blue," "Ilompty Dumpty," &c. Thl representations were capitally carried ow. At the close of the operetta, the Rev. J. R. Matthews said he was very glad of the opportunity of meeting them once more on an occasion like that, aftar a year's hard work. They hal a good many prizes, AS they could see, on the table, which had been earned by at- tendance and lessons, and to some extent be good con duct. However, it was said it VCIA "tever too rate to mend, and he should be very glad indeed if fathers and mothers, and Sunday school teachers and scholars would think about that, and see if they could no.. do stmething, towards imoroving on • that point. TEE MEMBERS' DINNER AT 'Ma WORICROME. The Dining Committee's recrirnmendations regarding the providing of dinners at the workhouse for members of the Board, were read by the Clerk. It was proposed that in lieu of a hot lunch tieing provided as previously, a cold lunch should be substituted for which each mem- ber who partook of it, should contribute one shilling, as formerly. The amount paid for out-relief at Run- corn during the fortnight was £95, compared with £B5 during the same time the previous year. Thera was also a slight increase in the amount paid for out-relief in the other districts of the Dnian. RUGBY. WARRINGTON v. SALFORD'. Warrington made their first acquaintance with Sal- ford for the present season on Saturday. The Warring- ton team had not previously played a • single match during the present year, and therefore, when the severe frost broke up last week, it was with a feeling, of relief on the part of the football enthusiasts. Saturday was anything hut an ideal day, of course, but still football could be played without danger to neck or limb. Sal- ford have been fortunate in being able to play during the frosty weather, and therefore, although these matches were with clubs of an inferior class to War- rington, the club was able to work off all stiffness and superabundant flesh, caused by their suspension, pre- paratory to tackling clubs of sterner stuff. The weather on Saturday was wretched in the extreme, and was altogether oppoeed to good football. The approaches to the New Barnes enclosure, as the Salford ground is termed, were of a fearful character. In fact, if there , had been much more mud and water, it would have been necessary to have swum through it. The football ground hid been protected by a large quantity of straw, and, therefore, was not as bad as was to be expected. During the whole of the match the rain was coming down pretty quickly, and, therefore, at the finish, the players presented the appearance of being half drowned, and of being of the pachydermatous genus, who are so fond of wallowing In mud. There was not an extraordinary crowd present, in consequence of the weather, the attendance number- ing between 2,000 and 3,000. MP:, Mrixon effieieeed as referee, and the following were the teams which were under his supervision t—Warrington—Bescow, full beck ; Burton, Heesom,Mnoree, and Barber, three• quarters; Foden, and Bennett, half backs; Turner (captain), • Jolley, Dakin, Houghton, Barrett, Savage, 'Bailey, and Taylor forwards. There was no return to Tuner's kick, which went over the line, and thus a minor was conceded the first minute by Salford. WARRINGTOW,T. MARY'S v. L. & N.-W. Locos.—Pleved on the St. Mary's ground in dull weather before a fair number of spectators. Plinston took the place of F. Hampson at back. The homesters won the toss, Hill starting for the Locos., who were the first to attack. The Saints played up determinedly, and before lone T. Bennett scored, Roughley linding a neat goal. From 1 the drop-out the game was hotly contested, and gradu- ally the visitors were forced back, from a scrimmage near the line Hieginbettom secured, dashed through the , thick of his opponents in grand style, and scored, Roughley failing to convert. Aroused by this reverse the Locos. played up ceneiderahly, but to no Avail, when from a rush by the Saints' forwards Thornton mulled in a dangerous position, and Thomas scored the third try for the Saints, G. Httmpson failing at goal. Nothing more occurred up to half-titne, when the Saints were leading by one goal two tries to nil. Re- starting, with the wind in favour of the Locos., they at once pressed, took the ball down the field, where Warburton was forced to save. Play continued to be of an even character until T. Bennett broke away from the scrimmage and scroed-his second try. Thomas doing the needful. From the drop-out the Locos. appeared worn out, the Saints having it :all their own way, and from a scrimmage Bennett passed to Rutter, who scored a try, the goal-kick failing. A minute later Plinston accepted a pass and walked in under the poste, as no attempt was made to stop him. Roughley landing a third goal, and when the whistle sounded the Saints retired winners of a rather one-sided game by three goals three tries to nil. WARRINGTON ROVERS V. Sr. BARNABAS.—This match was played on the ground of the former,and the ground being in a bad rendition the Rovers took the shine out of the St. Barnabas by 2 tries to one. RUNCORN V. STOCKPORT.—These Cheshire rivets played their return match at Ruocorn on Saturday. The first match at Stockport ended in a drawn game, so the contest was all the more interesting. The ground at Runcorn was in a very bad spate, which rendered the play and the men miserable. It was nearly 3.30 when the players turned out as follows :—Runcorn: S. Houghton, back ;T. Warder, W. Gayter, J. Butter- worth and W. Gregory,three-quarter backs; W. Pendia- bury and J. Faulkner, half-eecks ; W. Faulkner, A. Taylor, W. Langley, j. Pendlebury, S. Welkner, 11. Partner, F. Gayter, and R. Lightfoot,forwatds. Stock- port : Alcock, back ; !Seeley. Savilte, Chorlton, and Worsley, three-quarter baeks ; Norris and Roberts, half backs ; Bailey, Beard, Moreton, Gibson, Wrigley,King, Lord, and Mottershead, forwards. Faulkner started, I and Saville made a good return, Houghton being well held close to the touch line. King, Bailey, and Motters- head made an effort to rush the ball towards the home goal. Warder, however. changed the venue, and play of a dull nature followed until the home backs, en- livened matters by some cross ground passing. Play of a give.and-take nature followed, several efforts being made to break through the stubborn defence of Houghton. Helf-time came with no score. After the Interval the home team showed more determined play, and several raids on the Steokport goal should have been attended with more success. Bailey started, and Houghton returned the ball by a magnificent kick to the Stockport twenty-five. One splendid effort by several ef the home forwards forced Aloe* to kick dead. Is the game progressed it was thought by the spectators that there would be no score, until the continued attack by the home side raised their hopes in which they were not disappointed, as J. Faulkner made good gr mod, and passing timely to is brother, W. Faulkner w ' e with judgment, threw to Butterworth, the latter reedteti over,scorine a capital try. The goal kick failed.' F flowing this 'Runcorn were nearly across the line eetin, the game ending with play on the Stockport line. Final : Runcorn, one try, three minors ; Stockport,, nothing. RUNCORN V. A pretty passing movement by the whole of the visiting backs saw the game close to the home lines. Haelam gave relief, but it was only momentary, as from a pack close to the line Woreleverd gave a sharp pass to Clarke, who dodged finely over. The hotnesters hardly realized that a try had been scored. Dinveband took the place and made a gallant effort to secure the additienal points but the ball just passed outside. From the drop-out the heat, forwards initiated a raid which Jolley promptly ended by a fine kick, which foond touch. The home team now tried their hand at paesine, but Brown mull- , ing, Rencern coickbe eased tee pressure, and hand to hand passing foilowed,only to See West held a few yards from the home lines. A similar effort followed a moment : later, but both Myers and D Invabend failed to hold the greasy ball. C. Goodall and fleathcote dribbled down, aril the ball was taken over the Runcorn line, but West raced up and just managed to kick dead in the nick of time. Kicking oet, titoekpert made another raid, but Wend werd dribbled oot of danger. Runcorn continued to press, hut the Stockolrt hacks defended stehhernly, and the interval was reached with the snore Reneorn one try, Stockport nil. Haslarn commencel the second m4ety, and no return followed. For a considerable period the game was very moneton- ous, the hems team keying the ball eight. Unfortu- netely for Runcern Woodward had to leave the ground, Nickson taking his place at half-bank, and Antrobue filling the centre position. If otwithstarrling this draw- back the visitors mere titan held their own. Thus for the secend time this season Stockport had to bow to the superior prowees of Rtnrorn. The final 'more stood —Runcorn three points, Stoekport nil.

ORFORD BARRACIES.—ThiS match took place at Orford in had weather, the ground being very soft. The visitors winning the toss, the home team kicked off with the wind behind them. Orford at once attacked, and some grand passing resulted in P. Croft scoring two minutes from the start. From the kick off play was very even, and a grand forward rush by the Barracks enabled them to equalize. T. Povey, then scored the second goal for Orford The Barracks again pressed and scored. Orford now strove hard to gain the lead, and after a good run Weston scored. Half-time now arrivLd with the score—Orford,3; Orford Barracks, 2. Resuming the Barracks pressed. From a throw in, the Barracks rushed down and scored in the last two minutes, and the whistle blew with the scare 3 goals I each. Extra time was now played. 15 minutes each way. Both teams scoied in the first half. With only a few minutes to play, the Barracks tried their utmost to win,and from a throw in scored in the last minute. The whistle then sounded with the score—Orford Barracks, 5; Orf ord, 4.
F IRST ANNUAL MEETING OF THE WARRINGTON CHRIST [AN POLICE ASSOCIATION.
INTERESTING SPEECHES. On Monday evening the first annual tea in con nection with the above, Association was held in the Masonic Rom', Bold-street, when there was a fair no mber of

policemen present. After the tea had been disposed of, a public meeting was held in the M asonic Hill, at which there was a very large attendance. On the platform there were the Mayor (rdisirman), Dr. T. Starkey Smith, J.P. (presi- dent), R 'Vg T.J. Madden (St. Luke's Ehurch,Liverpool), F. W. Willis (Rector of Warrington), B. Percival. J. Davies, and J. Cooill (of Warrington), and Rev. Mr. Burnes (Liverpool). Amongst those present in the audi- ence were the Mayoress (Mrs. James Fairclough), Mr. and Mrs. John F sirclough), the Rev. E. T. and Mrs. Reed, Mrs. and Miss Gornall, Mrs. J. Yonge, and Miss

Bradbury. Miss BESSIE Durros (secretary), who en entering the room was loudly applauded. read letters or telegrams apologising for unavoidable absence, from the following gentlemen :--Mr. Z. Armitage, J.P.' Mr..B. J. Guest. J.P., Mr. T. Bir-hall, J.?, Councillors Henry Roberts. J.P., Win. Piernoint, IP., Mr. R. Garnett, J Y., Revs. J. Birtlan J. Yonge, G. D. Mason, and Mr.

H. Taylor. P.C.M. Miss [hereon said it was a little more than twelve months ago that that branch of the Christian Police As- sociation was started. The Association was doing its work in almost all lands. Miss Gurney, the moving spirit of the whole Association, was at present making a voyage round the world, and the speaker hoped that it would net be long hefore she was back. With regard to their own work, Miss Dutton said that She herself had had the friendly support of most of the police force. They commenced the work with a weekly Bible class, and every six weeks or two months, as the case might be, they had had an open meeting to which they had invited all the wives and friends of the police force, and had always had a very pleasant meeting. One meeting took the form of a tea,and they had a very enjoyable evening. What they wanted was more of the police force to join them, but still their increase of memhership thooeh slovv.had been steady. (Applause.) The Rey. T. J. MADDEN was sorry to say that he was "very well known to the nolice" and fir prii lential rel. sens he thought it would he well to " keel in with them" ; as they (the audienee) never knew what might happen in this uncertain world. (Laughter.) The only consolation that his wife gave him was that she hoped thstlkhen the police saw him coming home late they might "run him in," and it washer opinion that he wanted a " casual" yard and not a home. Hence he came to keep in with toe police and was in thehabit of speal-ing with them in Liverpool, and next week he was going to Londog NS keep an eye upon them there. He hoped that he miizht never be taken up for wan- dering abotit without any visible means of support." He was easily impssed upon—especially by ladies—and when their secretary came to him, he agreed to come ; it was part of his nationality and with all the chivalry of an Irishman he was ready to do and dare for a lady. Be was pleased to he there because he thought that the reason for the existence of their association was that it was intended to supplement the work of the churches and not to supplant it. They had missions for sailors because they could not often go to church ; they had missions for railway men because they had to work on Sundays, and they had one for policemen for even they had to keep an eye upon certain people even upon a Sunday, and so he thought it ways goal thing that they should remember that this work and kindred missions were intended only to supplement and not to take the place of the ordinary means of grace. A Christian police- man should, he said, be a cheerful Christian, and should show to the people about him that the religien of the Lord Jesus Christ was calculated to make them cheerful and happy. He had fovind many pslicemen to keep away from their Association because some of them, not I all, were a bit hard, gloomy an t stiff. It was no good giving a man their hand as if it was the tail of a dead cod-fish, (Laugher) and it was 'a pleasant thing to meet together before the meeting to have it cup of tea. Hp, himself, was one of those fanatical total abstainers. (Applause.) There was nothing about him that pro- claimed the fact except that he was healthy and strone and that was what teetotalers were. (Applause and laughter). The 8 hours' hill would be no use to him because he generally managed to put in 18 hours a day, all told. Policemen, he thought, should all be like the street lames—shining and bright—and appear the source of ofiverfuloess. Th v must, also be progressive and active Christians. (Loud applanse.) P.C.,P. T. TAYLOR (Manchcster) was there as a repre- sentative of the Manchester Christian P,Alf;.l Association and he was "hank'ul that thelr Chief Cens"a.hle was in sympathy with them.—P.C. Kays (Old Trafford) and the Rev. F. W. Willis (Warrington) also addressed the meeting, the latter cemeeiseratine with the police for their long and awkward hour and he. thanked them sincerely for all the kindness and courtesy they had shown him on many occasions. The Rey. B. PERCIVAL proposed a hearty vote of thanks to the Revs....- J. Madden, F. W. Willis, and the two policemen who had addressed the meeting.-e-l'he Rev. J. Davies seconded, and in supporting it Sergeant Smith said that Miss Dutton wan a noble leader and they I had always received encouragement from her, and he believed she was one of the noblest ladies in England. Sergeant Row oothato ales supported the motien , and endorsed what the last speaker had said. The motion was then put to the meeting and carried unanimously.—The Rev. F. W. Willis responded on behalf of Mr. Madden and himself, and said it was encouraging to see a lady like Miss Dutton there, taking an interest in such an institution. The Rev. Mr. BURN! proposed a vote of thanks to the Mayor and the ladies and, gentlemen who had contri- buted to the evening's enjoyment. After the passing of the vote the Mayer replied by expressing his pleasure at being present. Miss Dutton was a lady whotr. he had always respected, and whatever she di I she did tt.or- oughly and well. He was sorry to see so few policemen present. A policeman's life he took to be an arduous one. He concluded by exhorting them to always tell the truth in the witness box. and thanked them for the . vote they had given him.—Dr. T. Starkey Smith also re- vonded. He thought the meeting had been a very en- joyable and instructive one, and calculated to improve the position of the policemen. During the evening mnsical selections were played by She orchestra of the People's Service, conducted by Mr. F. Pendleberse The meeting concluded with singing and prayer. .

Result : Parish, two goals; Penk4th, one goal. Fa RISWORTri V. WAURINGTON ST. MetteS.—This match was played on a Water covered groond.al',Farnworth,on, Saturilly, before a moderate gate. Both teams mustered strongly. Farnworth started and the visitors ran up, but were repelled by a stout dc_ifence. The home team returned the compliment, and G. The Newton half hacks, who were playing a stront, game, rarely allowed the-Albion& opportunity for showing what they could do,-and Rogers, the centre' half, sending in a good shot that hit the crossbar, R. div.head: ANOTHER COLLIERY DISASTER.
div.p: ANOTHER COLLIERY DISASTER.

GREAT LOSS OF LIFE. Although crest progress was made with the relie operations at the AlMley colliery on Wednesday, none if the entombed men have yet been rescued alive. In- deed, as the night wore on heavy falls and obstructions were discovered, which, it is feared, may postpone the disdnvery of the men for another twelve hours. Hope for those in the Bft. sesn is wholly abandoned. It is known that they are even now under water. Two dad bodies were discovered during Tuesrl,v night and on Wednesday. An official list of those still in the pit puts the number at either seventy-five or seventy-eight. Of the thirty-five are married men end fifteen are lads. Fortunately all are members of the North Staffordshire Miners' Relief Fund. At midnight the men had been entombed sixty-six hours. At the Audley Colliery on Thursday, the search for the missing men was continued, but without any success. In the atternoon, owing to the presence of obstructions in the roadways, hope of rescuing. any -of the men alive was finally abandoned. The Coroner's inquest was opened on Thursday and adjourned.

APPLETON PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE.—This committee met at the Bridge Inn, Stockton Heath, on the 18th inst. and the minutes were submitted at the meeting of the Runcorn Rural Council held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Mr.' Joseph Knowles occupied the chair. It was decided that Mr. Joseph Knowles. member of the Rural District Council of Runcorn, and the members of the Appleten Parish Council, form the parochial committee. It was resolved on the motion of Mr. John Whitlow, seconded by Mr. Davenport that Mr. Joseph Knowles be appointed chairman of the committee until the 15th April. The Clerk read letters from the Town Clerk of Warrington in which he stated that he had laid the letter ol the Parochial cemmittee before his committee and he was entruated to inform them that the Manchester Ship Canal Company had closed the culvert or sluice referred to, without consulting the Corporation, and that the Corporation had requested the Company to re-open it. The sluice was not within the Borough and was not, he thought, a work authorised by the Act of 1885. The Warrington Rural District Council within whose district the work was situate would, he understood. deal with the matter. In a further letter the Town Clerk said the Council had passed a resolution asking the company to re-open the sluice or culvert in the New-road, at Wilderspool, and it ' would be a matter of arrangement between the Cor- poration and the company in an agreement now being made between them. A letter on the same subject was also read from Mr. Samuel Sutton, cleik of the Warring- ton Rural District Council, stating that when the autho- rity was responsible for the health of the inhabitants from the Cheshire side of the river it seemed to them im- perative to Pay regard to the state of the river. Now, the borough and the Runcorn Disti ict Council were al- most exclusively concerned, the Lancashire side con- sisting of agricultural lands for long distances from the river. At the same time he felt sure the Council would give to them and the C orporation all reasonable support in their enforcement of remedial measures.—Mr. Davenport called atten- tion to the manner in which the contractor for the removal of nightsoil,&c., executed the work, and stated that many of the receptacles were not emptied at all,and that all the work was not executed within the hours prescribed by the contract, and also that the nightsoil was left in the streets and roads for an unreasonable time. It was resolved that the Clerk write to the con- tractor on the matter. It was decided that the sum of £1 per annum be paid to the proprietor of the London Bridge Inn, for the use of the room for the meetings of the Committee.—The minutes were passed on the motion of Mr. Knowles, seconded bo Mr. Davenport.

LOCAL PARISH COUNCIL MEETINGS. L&TCHFORD WITHOUT. ' This Council met at the Baptist School, Wash-lane, on Monday evening. Mr, Percy Davies presided, and there were also present—the Rev. E. Moore, Messrs. William Plerpoint, John Lee, G. Nicholson, William Richer*son, and George Pilling. Mr. Davies thanked all present at the last meeting for appointing him their chairman. If he could do anything to help them in their work it:would aßord him pleasure. He thought the Parish Council Act, from what he knew of it, would not do much good in that parish, and they would not live very long, because the Warringtoa Corporation had applied to the Local Government Board for the borough boundary to be ex- tended so as to include part of that parish. He thought they were a pattern sort of parish, for there were very few that had not eat a publichouse or church. He had been promised a plan of the parish by the Borough Sur- veyor, and he thought they should do what they could to promote the interests of Latchford Without, I The Chairman presented copies of the "Parish Councils 1 Gozotte " to the meeting, and asked whether it would be wise to order copies to be taken regularly, at theexnense of the Council. It was ultimately decided tn accept the copies as samples, and then settle the matter at-the next ineeting.—The Clerkread a letter from the Town Clerk re the borough extension, stating that Warriegton Cor- poration hid applied to the Local Government Board for power to take in a part of that township, and asking for a deputation from that Umncil to meet the Town Council on the-matter. Mr. Pierpoint thought it would he to the interests of the parish to be absorbed by the Corporation. They had only one policeman at present, and he (Mr. Pierpnint) had to employ a watchman night and day to watch over his property. He begged to move that this Parish Council itrrange to meet the Corporation of Warrington, at the Town Hall, the day of meeting to be left with the Chairman. Mr. Lee seconded, and it was carried unanimously. This was all the business. GREAT SANKEY. The members of the Great Sankey Parish Council met in the Boardroom, Great Sankey Schools, on Monday. The following members were present—Mr. W. P. Skel- ton (chairman), Mr. H. Bate (vice-chairman), Mr. Wm. L. Gorse, Mr. Thomos Halton. Mr. Thomas Kilshaw,Mr. G. Thompson, Mr. J. Wright (assistant overseer), and Mr: Grirnshaw (a member of the Little Sankey Parish Council.) Mr. James Faircloueh Was absent on account. of sickness. Mr. Gorse spoke at some length of the great necessity of lamps on the Liverpool-road from Houghton's Wire Works to Sankey Chapel House, and proposed that Mr. Joseph Wright (clerk) • be instructed to write to the Clerk of the County Council, reqeesting their financial assistance to cerry out the suggestion. Six lamps would be ample for the present.—The resolution was seconded by Mr. Bate and carried unanimously.—Mr. George Thompson proposed, and it was seconded by Mr. ITAton,that the dole of El per annum due to this parish from Mr. Warburton, Aria? Hail, he taken over for dis- tribution by this Council. Carried imanimously.—Mr. Halton proposed, and Mr. G. Thompson seconded, that the old parish chest be removed from the Chapel House Inn to the Board Schools, and that it be opened in the nresence of the members of the Council at their next meeting. The motioo was carried.—lt was proposed by Mr. Thompson, and unanimously resolved, that the Parish Council meet in the Board Schools every third Monday in each mouth at seven p.m. WESTON.

ACCIDENT. —Horace Sory, OF Lancaster, belonging to the schooner Twin Brothers, lying at Weston Point, met with a somewhat serious accident on Saturday evening. He was chopping some wood with an adz, which slip- ping, cut through his boot, making a gash in his foot. He was taken to the surgery of Dr. McKenzie, at Run- corn, who stitched the wound. The man is progressing satisfactorily.

SCIENCE, AND TH MAN iN TETE STREET. Sir,—l appear to have been unfortunate enough to have reused the wrath of our friend Felix to more than "summer's" heat—or fever heat—nay even unto 212 de- grees and boiling over. Ah ! me infelix ! Unhappy that lam ; that I cannot see my way to accept Mr. Su Tuners' very peculiar reasoning upon his very peculiar Botany. I have before said that his Botany is not of this world, now his method (or want of it) and his notions of experimentation are distinctly of this world, they are easentially those of the" man in the street." He evidently is quite innocent of the value and necessity of analysis as a means of getting to " know." Our I friend's proclivities in this direction may have suffered in early blight by his ma spanking him for cutting open the bellows to see where the wind came from. This would account for his distaste for scientific experiment- ation. Hence we have his crude and crass methods of experimentation in vogue with the man in the street whose inscience leads him to prefer to look at things in the bulk, not knowing the absolute need of analysis—taking to pieces—to got to know the nature ed things. Do this with a grain of wheat and it is found to consist of a small living part and a much larger dead part. A. grain of whent.as such.is not a living organism, hence it cannot die. But Mr. Summers asks his readers to " pall up" a six inch wheat plant ! to see whether it—the imed— be not dead!! Dead, yes eead as a her- ring, but unlike the herring it never was alive. Let me try to aid Me. Summers' comprehension by an illustra- tion. Let him go to his ash-pit and contemplate there the ruins of former fires. Those ashes are dead—dead as the seed wheat, and they, like the seed, have pa.sed through a chemical transformation—and we have quite as muck warrant to say that the coal was alive and is dead se we have to say this for the seed wheat. Mr. F. S. displays a very superior ability in leaving the subject in hand and proving something else. Hence he compares the many budded root "of the " scutch" (Tritiouin repeat) with the single germei Need wheats, just as the man in the street might. Now a " root "of the couch grass, will produce just as many plants as there are eyes in the " root "—just as a potato will—so many and no more. Like the seed it is dead all but the "eyes." Now, belt noted, that what the man in the street calls a "root," in couch grass and the potato, is ot a root at all—but an underground stem with buds —or eves; and if, by some miracle, it came to he alive, and lived to the age of Methuselah,it would " put forth" no more plants than it posseved eyes. I am pleased to see that Mr. Summers now concedes all that I ever asked for on this mbject. Ile now says that he heartily endorses the fact that the dead pert of the seed cannot die, and that other authority on this question—" Ben Cheyill "—distinctly averred as much of the living part, se) here I must ask our hortatory philosopher, what it is ia the seed wheat that does die ? Suppose we now get to the bed-rock of the facts, neglecting the tangle in which our friend has involved it? I have read in some old boek.and it has been again and again reiterated by men sworn te maintain this de- lusion,that" except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and lie . . it will not quicken." Now, I claim to I have proved to demonstration, I. That the seed need not touch the ground in order to "quicken." and IL That nothing—living et dead—dies in this quickening. That this is ample disproof of the seed-dying dogma will he evident to any one who knows the value of evieence. But these facts, against which the science of Warringten kas nothing to advance, is disputed by our celestial botanist, who draws his facts from an over- active " inner consciousness." Should Mr. Sum- mers elect still further to favour us- with more specimens of his superteundane botany there Are two things I would advise him to avoid. Let him remember that Brevity is the soul of wit," when he is inclined to be so excruciatingly facetious. In one untouched by Momus, a prolix, cumbersome affectation of jocularity may lead to laughter in his readers—but this will be at rather that with him by those who can appreciate his " nounderings." Again, when he does me the honour of quoting my words, would he kindly take care to do PO accurately, and not misleadingly ? I never denied " that the body of the seed is all used up in forming the foundation of the plant." I have mserted that in nature this was so—but that it was not an " indispin s- Dile condition "for the " quickening " of the embryo, which could be effected aatincially without any such " death." And now a few words upon the general aspect of this question. The Christianity of to-day is charseterised by that " Molluscoue condition which has not a kick left in it." Like certain pulpy palypea it may be dismembered, pushed punished or even eviscerated—turned inside nut—without incon- venience. "Christianity up te date" has no "essentials " ; but it has many "gelatinous "adherents equally devoid of essential principlee—encial and religi- ous humbugs—who with the acquirements nf the nineteenth century at their command, faiu to believe
THE EXAM NEft. SATURI,AY, JANUARY 26 1895

div.head: ATHLETICS.
div.p: ATHLETICS.
NOTES ON GAMES AND

FOOTBALL. The Warrington team were able to play for the first time during the present year, on Saturday, arid had for their opponents the team which has caused so much attention to be paid to it, owing to its having been sus- panded,and also having caused the suspension of Wigan, and indirectly of Radcliffe. The Salford team have been extremely lucky in their suspension, for during that time, they had ten away matches, and only two home matches, and commencing with their first match after their suspension, they have seven home matches in suc- cession. In fact, the time of suspension might have been arranged for, to cause less expense to the club. I should not be surprised indeed, to find that Salford have been the gainers by it, as, leaving out the matches which were cancelled, they will have during the present seas,m sixteen home, and only ten away matches. On terms like these, I don't think some clubs would object to being suspended a little, each season.

This is in striking contrast with Wigan, who during their period of suspension had arranged for seven home, and six away fixtures, and amongst the home fixtures were such popular ones as Halifax, Runcorn, Broughton Rangers, St. Helens, and Widnes. The loss is indeed grew; to the Wigan club, and lam afraid that it will seriously affect their exchequer. It is a little singular that Warrington were not affected by the suspension of Leigh,Salford or Wigan,their fixtures not coming during the period when these clubs were doing "time."

The Salford Club coin tnenced their season afresh on New Year's Day, and unlike most of the clubs in the county Palatine, they had been able to play off all their fixtures up to data. owing to protecting their ground with straw. They were thus able to get their arms and legs in proper working order, while Warrington were vegetating in enforced idleness.

By the way, I think the Salford club ought to agitate for an improvement in the approaches to their en- closure which rejoices in the name of New Barnes. On a day like Seturday, when the rain came down in tor- rents, the state of the toad was something abominable. There was no parapet, and therefore everyone was com- pelled to walk over the ankles in mud, for almost a quarter of a mile. The state of one's shoes by the time the field was reached can be better imagined than described. Notwithstanding the state of weather and road, over 2,000 wended their way to the field.

The game was a very keenly contested one. War- rington were undoubtedly the superior lot with the ex- ception of ability in the art of scoring. It was not very often that Salford were really dangerous in comparison with Warrington, and yet they were able to gain the day, though only by the goal kick. It would not be too much to say that Warrington had two thirds the game. It is a very disappointing feature of the play that notwithstanding good play in the open, they cannot do the needful when the time comes. Instead of only ' one try, they ought to have scored three at least.

To come to the players, I will commence with the forwards. Warrington forwards were much the superior to their opponents until the last twenty minutes of the game, when they appeared to get disorgacised, and it was during this time that Salford scored their winning goal. During the greater part of the game, however, they heeled out, and screwed the scrimmages very much better than Salford. The Salford forwards are not a very heavy lot, but they know how to rush, and do not fail take advantage:of the slightest relaxation on the part of their opponents. The tries on each side were scored by forwards, for Warrington by Turner, and for Salford by Brierley, and this emphasises the fact that the game was chiefly a leeward game, the state of the ground militating against aa open game.

Owing to the superior hoeing out on the part of War- riagten,the visiting half-backs had better chances than their visa vie, but they did take quite sufficient advan- tage of this. It will be noticed that the halves chosen— Bate and Nevins—could not play and therefore the "A" team half-backs—Bennett and Poden—were chosen. They did not do amiss, considering that they were in strange company.

The threequarter line on each rale were fairly matched. Barber and Burton at each wing were very speedy, add tackled well, and Barber was very unfor- tnnate, very early in the game, in losing possession just on the point of scoring. Eleesom was very safe, and defended weli,as also did fdoores,who was always in the thick of the fray. Boseow made some daring saves,and played with his usual form. Rangeley and Barrett were a capital pair smarm the Salford threequarters, and Rangeley's fine kick at goal was the means of giving his side the victory.

The game would have counted as a Lancashire Rugby League fixture but for the misdeeds of Salford, but con- sidering the result, Warrington have not much need to be sorry about it. There were only two fixtures in this competition on Saturday, the most interesting being the meeting of the leaders, Oldham and Tyldesley. As I stated as my opinion last week, Tyldeslev were too good for Oldham in the forward rank, and though they only won by a try to nil, they ought to have won by a larger score. In fact, the bail was taken over the line time after time, only to be brought into play again, for some informality. This defeat will seriously imperil Oldham's chances of retaining the cup. The other match between Broughton Rangers and Rochdale Hornets resulted in a win for the latter by the same narrow majority of one try to nil.
Below I give the result of the Cup Competition up to date:— _ .
For Agst.

Phi. Won. Lost. Drn. G.T. d.T.Pts Tyldesley Oldham St. Helens 6 . 3 . 3 . 0 . 4 6... 2 5... 6 Warrington Rochdale Hornets hwinton 6 . 1 3 . 2 . 1 3... 3 6... 4 Broughton Rangers 6 . 1 . 4 . 1 . 3 2... 6 7... 3 Leigh (on September 19), blalford (October 16), and Wigan (November 13), having been suspended br professionalism, will not take any part in the competition this season. '

To-day. Rochdale Hornets will be tackled at Rochdale, and as this is a league match, it is important that the Warrington team should strive with all their might and main to Rain the verdict. The result of the first meeting was a victory for Warrington by the narrow majority of a try to nil. Should Warrington win on Saturday,they would reach the third place in the league, in fact they would even if they drew. If on the contrary they lose. they will drop to the fifth, and possibly even to the sixth position owing to point average. It ig, therefore, very important that Warrington should win to-day.

To cope with the Hornets at Rochdale, the following team has been chosen to represent Warrington :—Full back. J. 13,scow ; three-quarters, Barber, Heesom, Moores, and Burton ; half hacks, Bate, and Nevins; forwards. Turner, Jolley, Dakin, Taylor, Berry, r Bailey, floughton, and Barrett.

Unlike their seniors the" A" team were victorious on Saturday, The Salford "A " team is a capital junior team. and therefore to beat them by two tries to nil was a good performance. I hope that the "A "team will continue the second half of the season as they have begun. The first half was not a very successful one and could be very much improved, as likewise could also the record of the first team.

St. Mary's gained an easy victory over the London and North-Western Locomotives on Saturday, winning by no less than three goals, three tries to nil. The "Saints " were as superior as the sclfire indicates, and almost played the Locomotives to a standstill. Stockton Heath managed to make a draw with Widnes " A" team, which is better than the Warrington " A " team cmild do. The " Chemical team has an extremely successful season up to the pres-nt, and Stockton Heath did a very good performance by making a draw with them.

Runcorn football enthusiasts should be highly de- lighted with the performances of both their first and " A "teams on Saturday, for each succeeded in coming out of the encounter, victorious. The premier team played their first engagement for this year " at home' when they had for their opponents, Stockport. Beth teams are recognized as being about the best exponents of the Ruby game in Cheshire and it was anticipated that a good and ovenly-contested game would be the result. There was one drawback and that was the wretched state of the ground. The only point registered , in the match was the try scored ty Butterworth for the home team which was the finishing touch of a grand effect to score by the Runcornians. Stockport struggled bravely to equalise, hut withaut avail, and again had to submit to ths superior prowess of the Runcorn team. At Stockport, the " A " team of that town endeavoured te lower the victorious colours of the Runcorn " A " team, but the Runcorn lads proved just to. good for them, winning by three poiats to nil, which, singular to say, was exactly the sane score between the first teams at Runcorn.

PoreLan CONCERTS. —The weekly concert was held in the Newfield Institute en Saturday night. There was a crowded audience. The concert, which was an excellent one, had been got up by Mrs. Ernest Crosfield. Songs, banjo and mandoline solos, &c., were given by Mr.Warrington, Miss N. Cookson, Mr. Dickson,Mr.Peter Holt, Mrs. Ernest Crosfield, and the :Misses Todhuater. The entertainment was brought to a close by a dialogue in character by Mrs. Ridgway and Mrs. Ernest Cros- field. THEFT OF MIITTON.—Poare Jackson, labourer, Lymm, was charged at the Lymm Police Courtons Sat. with steal- ing half a shoulder of mutton,value 23., the property of Hugh Harrison, between 3 and 6 p.m. on the previous day.—Harry Lee, apprentice to Mr. Forest, blacksmith, said he was in the smithy opposite Mr. Harrison's shop, and noticed the prisoner passing and re-passing the shop for about ten minutes. He then saw him put it his hand under the window, and take the mutton and put in his pocket. Prisoner then ran away round the mill.—Serg- eant Garner stated that he received information of the nitn about 8.15 p.m. ort, t he night of the 18th inst. and apprehended the prisoner. On searching his pockets, he found a small piece of fat in one of them. On being charged with stealing the mutton he replied that he knew nothing about it.—Prisoner Aaid he did not remember taking it.—As it was his first offence, he was fined 305., in deL.ult of payment,l4 days' imprisonment. The money was paid.

ROUSH COMMITTBE. Mr. DAWNS moved and Mr. CLARKS Seconded the pass- sing of the Rouse Committee's minutes, which stated that at a meeting held on January 11th, Mr. Davies had been elected chairman, and Mr. Clarke, vice-chairman of the committee until the annual meeting in April.

SCHOOLS COMMITTEE. This committee reported that Mr. William Houghton had been appointed chairman, and Mr. •..I. Jolley vice- chairman of the committee--The minutes were adopted in the motion of the CHALSMAN, seconded by Mr. A. .1. Jowa. _ _ _

SATISFACTORY STATE OF FADOATB scrioora. The Crates said that he had had a set of queries te answer from the Local Government Board. In reply to the query with regard te Padgate Schools, he had said that during the twelve years which the children had been there, there bad only been three deaths, and those were of poor children, who came into the school in a very delicate state. The number of inmates ia the Infirmary exclusive of imbeciles and lunatics was also asked for, and the reply was 54 male and 47 female. Th•re were two paid nurses for the day, and One for the night. There were no imbeciles and lunatics. With regard to the number of Guardians, etc., he had replied that previous to the election there were 30 members all gentlemen. There were now 27 gentlemen. and one lady. The number of old members re-elected was 14. sVOGHSTIONS BY A LOCAL GOVBENBENT Boas) OFFICER. Mr. JENNER POST an inspector of the Local Govern.? merit board, who was present, then made some observa- tions with regard to a visit to the House paid by him- self and a brother-inspector, Mr. Monsen, in September, and also if a visit by Dr. Fuller,a medical officer for the Local Government Boar& He thought that all poisons in the infirmary should be in peculiar shaped bottles, and not merely have the red label on marked" poison." —Dr. BaSIDB said that was dene.—Continuing, Mr. Fusr said that he understood that religiousservices were attended in the town by the inmates. He thought that it would he as well to send the children who were in the house to Sunday school, if there was one within a reasonable distance belonging te their denomination. He also thought that there should be a better supply of water in order to extinguish fires should they break out, as it was generally the first few minutes which were the most important. He considered that better apparatus should be obtained than the Canvas shoots for fire escapes. They weuld act very well for able bodied men, but not for aged people. Mr. Puller, in his report. upon his visit, had said that it was a matter of regret that there was such a poor infirmary for the Union. Many of the wards were inappr,.0....1 for use as sick wards. He regretted that there was no paid nurse in the infectious wards. He paid a high compliment to the matron, who he said was a highly efficient and energetic officer, and he also spots in terms of praise of her daughter, the assistant matreo.—Mr. DAVIES said that he would be extremely obliged if Mr. Fust would point out how they were to get every sug- gestion carried out. Some alteration would have to be made, but the old committee was always averse to spending too much money. He hoped the new com- mittee would he more generous than the old one. He was living in hopes that they would have offices in the town, and then they would be able to utilise the Beard- room and offices as part of the workhouse. He promised Mr. Poet that his suggestions should have their seriouS consideration.—The CIIATEMAN wished the Clerk would draw up a statement of the rent paid for their various offices in the town. He thought that that money would more than pay the interest for the site of offices in a central position in the town.—The CLERK said that the most necessary thing was a new infirmary, and that would have to be faced before they did anythiag else.— The CIAAIRMAN said that this question had been dropped the last year or two, pending the expected changes with regard te the Cheshire parishes. That was the principal reason for deferring the question.—Mr. Fes said that the question of providing a new infirmary would have to be met. The manner of completing the scheme was the main thing to la! looked to—rise subject then dropped.
